a_rows_sample.anchor: How do we ensure that a KnowledgeOS decision gate can never authorize a state that violates a mandatory invariant?
a_rows_sample.statement: Three distinct questions must be separated: Question 1 (Epistemic) 'Do we have sufficient knowledge?'; Question 2 (Logical) 'Are the decision conditions internally consistent?'; Question 3 (Governance/safety) 'Is the resulting action permitted?'. Therefore SufficientKnowledge != ValidDecision != AuthorizedAction. This distinction is stated as fundamental, moving the investigation from 'do we know enough' to 'is the decision formally admissible'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Post,Temporal,Evidence)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a first-version Decision Contract DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Post, Temporal, Evidence): preconditions (what must already be true, e.g. IdentityConfirmed=True), invariants (what must never be violated, e.g. ProductionChange=>Approved, VoteCount<=MaximumAllowed, explicitly a domain constraint not merely evidence), authorization requirements, required postconditions, timing constraints, and assurance requirements. Preconditions and invariants are kept strictly separate: a precondition asks whether the world is ready for the operation; an invariant asks whether the operation is allowed to produce a state violating a protected property.

a_rows_sample.anchor: {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}
a_rows_sample.statement: Borrows Hoare-logic style {P} d {Q} (if precondition P holds, execution of d should produce a state satisfying Q) and applies it as {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}. Immediately argues ordinary Hoare logic is insufficient for KnowledgeOS because it additionally needs Evidence, Uncertainty, Authority, TemporalValidity and Provenance -- so the KnowledgeOS decision contract must extend the classical Hoare form.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Admissible = Pre and Invariant and Assurance and Authorization
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Admissible(d,K,t) iff Pre(d,K,t) and Invariant(d,K,t) and Assurance(d,K,t) and Authorization(d,K,t) -- a strict conjunction. Worked example: if Pre=True, Assurance=True, Authorization=True but Invariant=False, then Admissible=False regardless; 'there must be no averaging' across the conjuncts (i.e. no compensable weighted-sum scoring of admissibility conditions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: DC(d)=<P,I,A,E,Q,T,O>; Admissible as six-way conjunction
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates and extends the Decision Contract as DC(d) = <P,I,A,E,Q,T,O> where P=preconditions, I=invariants, A=authorization, E=evidence requirements, Q=epistemic sufficiency, T=temporal constraints, O=postconditions; and Admissible(d,K,t) iff P(K,t) and I(K,t) and A(K,t) and E(K,t) and Q(K,t) and T(K,t), with Execute(d) only then permitted.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision evaluation != decision execution; dry-run capability
a_rows_sample.statement: States that KnowledgeOS should conceptually perform Evaluate(d) before Execute(d), so Decision evaluation != Decision execution. The architecture should support Evaluate(d,K) without actually executing d, enabling simulation, review, what-if analysis, governance checks and AI planning; extends to a counterfactual decision WhatIf(Execute(d)) with estimated PostState(d), flagged as important for the later causal-reasoning formalization.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Safety gate pipeline: Plan->Evaluate->Validate->Authorize->Safety Gate->Execute->Observe Outcome
a_rows_sample.statement: For consequential operations, depicts a pipeline Plan -> Evaluate -> Validate -> Authorize -> Safety Gate -> Execute -> Observe Outcome, with the rule that the side effect must occur after the gate. Applies this to bound AI agents: an AI agent may propose d but should not automatically bypass Admissibility, so AIProposal -> DecisionEvaluation -> PolicyGate; states the architecture rule 'AI may propose; the governed system decides whether the proposal is admissible', and explicitly rejects Trust(AI)=True in favor of Capability(AI) constrained by Policy -- an AI agent's authority is explicitly bounded.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 42 (all PASS)
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests against the Step 42 model, all recorded PASS: (1) epistemic requirements pass but authorization fails => Admissible=False; (2) authorization passes but a hard invariant fails => Block; (3) all conditions known except a safety-critical invariant => Block/Unknown per policy, never automatic authorization; (4) a valid transition from a valid state preserves the invariant; (5) a transition that would violate a domain invariant is rejected; (6) a required approval expires before execution => decision becomes inadmissible; (7) evidence used by a decision is revoked => dependency closure identifies affected assurance and decisions; (8) an AI proposes an action violating a governance rule => proposal may be recorded but execution is blocked; (9) new evidence disproves an earlier assumption => existing assurance can be downgraded/revoked; (10) a decision is evaluated without execution => dry-run result has no side effect; (11) an invariant belongs to bounded context BC_A => KnowledgeOS does not silently redefine it from BC_B; (12) a decision passes technical assurance but lacks governance authorization => TechnicallySupported=True, Authorized=False, therefore Execute=False.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Step 42 verdict and seven closing principles
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 42 -- PASS and restates seven principles as the step's headline results: (1) Sufficient Knowledge != Valid Decision; (2) Valid Decision != Authorized Action; (3) Unknown safety state must not silently become safe; (4) Hard invariants are non-negotiable; (5) AI proposal != authorized execution; (6) Every consequential decision should have an explicit contract; (7) Evidence invalidation must propagate through decision dependencies.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Second-order decision contract DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Evidence,Post,Effects); horizon-dependent reachability safety; delayed effects
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Step 42 decision contract to DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Evidence, Post, Effects), where Effects(A) = {E_1,...,E_n} covers both ExpectedEffect and PotentialSideEffects, so the system should evaluate not only the immediate postcondition but what important downstream states an action could create. Defines horizon-dependent reachability safety: an action A is safe only if Reach_H(S,A) intersect S_unsafe = empty for horizon H -- safety cannot usually be proven for t->infinity, so a finite horizon (e.g. 24h or 30 days) must be chosen, making Safety(d,H) horizon-specific (an action safe for H=1 day may be unsafe for H=2 years). Some actions have Lag(A,Y)>0 (e.g. ArchitectureChange -> MaintenanceCost manifesting months later); represents delayed causality as Y_{t+tau}=f(A_t,...) with delay tau as part of the causal model; warns that a controller reacting before a previous action's effects become visible (A_t -> S_{t+tau} -> Decision_{t+tau+1}) can overcorrect, producing oscillation (Increase->Decrease->Increase->Decrease) even when each local decision appears rational -- 'the problem lies in the dynamic system', so the decision engine should consider EffectDelay, not merely EffectExists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge != Decision != Action; decision problem D=(K,A,Θ,U,C,R); expected utility argmax rule not a universal formula
b_rows_sample.statement: States Knowledge != Decision != Action: a decision needs objective, alternatives, constraints, risk, utility, authority beyond mere knowledge. Formalizes a decision problem D=(K,A,Theta,U,C,R) (knowledge, available actions, world states, utility, constraints, risk model), expected utility EU(a|K)=sum_theta P(theta|K)U(a,theta) (or the integral form), and the rule a*=argmax_a EU(a|K) -- explicitly qualified: this is not universally the correct decision rule (alternatives include minimax, constrained optimization, risk-sensitive utility, satisficing, lexicographic priorities, regulatory rules), so DecisionPolicy != UniversalMathematicalFormula; the Decision Context owns the meaning of DecisionPolicy, the mathematics supplies tools, the domain determines which is legitimate -- 'prevents mathematics from silently becoming business policy'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Experiments 1-5: underdetermined decision returns InsufficientDecisionBasis; ties; hard constraints vs preferences; risk limits; governance prohibition overrides utility
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: given K and A but no utility function, ChooseAction(K,A) must return Underdetermined/InsufficientDecisionBasis rather than inventing a decision -- PASS. Experiment 2: EU(a1)=EU(a2) yields a Tie, requiring an explicit tie-breaking rule if selection is mandatory -- PASS. Experiment 3: EU(a1)>EU(a2) but a1 not-in FeasibleActions means a1 cannot be selected; defines A_feasible={a in A: C(a)=True}, a*=argmax over A_feasible -- PASS, giving BestAction = BestFeasibleAction under the applicable decision policy, not simply HighestUtilityAction, and Constraint != Preference (a hard constraint C(a)=False removes a from A_feasible entirely, a preference only affects utility). Experiment 4: a risk policy Risk(a)<=R_max makes a high-EU action ineligible if it violates the risk limit -- PASS. Experiment 5: governance marking Forbidden(a1)=True excludes a high-utility a1 from A_feasible -- PASS, giving Decision = Knowledge + Objective + Constraints + Policy, and framing KnowledgeOS's question as 'what decisions are legitimate under knowledge, objectives, constraints, and authority' rather than a pure optimizer's max f(x).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision provenance object; risk measures (variance, VaR/ES) as domain-chosen, not universal
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines an auditable decision basis D=(KnowledgeSnapshot, Alternatives, Objective, Constraints, Policy, Model, SelectedAction, Rationale), with Rationale = f(Knowledge, Evidence, Policy, Objective, Risk), not merely 'AI recommended action A'. Notes a high-EU-but-catastrophic-downside action may be disfavored versus a slightly-lower-EU low-variance alternative by a risk-sensitive policy such as EU(a)-lambda*Var(U(a)), or domain-specific measures VaR_alpha/ES_alpha for financial-like domains -- 'KnowledgeOS should not impose one universal risk measure'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: AI proposal is not decision; proposal strength != decision authority (experiments 6-7)
b_rows_sample.statement: AIProposal -> DecisionEvaluation is retained (a proposal is not yet a Decision). Experiment 6: AI proposes a forbidden action a_f; Decision=Rejected -- PASS. Experiment 7: AI proposes a1 without sufficient decision basis; DecisionStatus=InsufficientBasis, not Approved -- PASS. Gives the epistemic boundary: Proposal strength != Decision authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Probability thresholds as policy, not mathematical truth; threshold sensitivity and robust (minimax) decision-making under model-set uncertainty
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: threshold=0.95, P(p)=0.94 gives ActionNotAuthorized -- PASS; notes a threshold is a policy, not a mathematical truth. Notes threshold-crossing at P(p)=0.951 may still be domain-prohibited if the uncertainty estimate is large, so a probability threshold alone may be insufficient. Introduces robust decision-making over a model set M (rather than optimizing a single expected value): a*=argmax_a min_{M in M} EU_M(a), 'a possible decision policy, not a universal one'. Distinguishes Aleatoric uncertainty (irreducible variability, e.g. manufacturing process randomness) from Epistemic uncertainty (incomplete knowledge/model limitations, e.g. little data about a new machine) -- additional measurements may reduce the latter but not the former.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EVSI makes information acquisition itself a governed decision; a controlled decision-learning loop; not all knowledge is decision-relevant
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines Expected Value of Sample Information EVSI = EU_with-sample - EU_current, and asks whether EVSI > cost(E) before acquiring additional measurement E, making information acquisition itself a decision. Formalizes the resulting loop K_t -> D_info -> E_new -> K_{t+1} as 'not a problematic cycle... a controlled decision-learning loop' giving KnowledgeOS active-learning capability. Experiment 10 (EVSI=0, positive acquisition cost): rational policy may choose not to acquire the information -- PASS, reinforcing Step 61: information can have IG>0 but EVSI=0, so not all knowledge is decision-relevant. Experiment 11: modest IG but large EVSI (an information source changes the optimal action despite modest uncertainty reduction) -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Richer typed Decision object; Selected != Authorized; Decision selection != Authorization; complete governed chain
b_rows_sample.statement: Strengthens Decision = (DecisionId, KnowledgeSnapshot, Objective, Alternatives, Constraints, Policy, RiskModel, DecisionRule, SelectedAlternative, Authority), 'much richer than decision=approve'. Decision status can be Proposed, Evaluated, Selected, Rejected, Expired, Superseded -- but Selected != Authorized: the system can determine a*=best feasible alternative without granting execution permission, giving Decision selection != Authorization. Experiment 12: Selected(a1)=True but Authorized(a1)=False must block execution -- PASS. Notes even Authorized(a1) does not mean Executed(a1) (a separate transition), giving the complete chain Knowledge -> Evaluation -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome, each arrow governed. States AI participates at multiple points (EvidenceExtraction, Hypothesis, DecisionProposal, RiskAnalysis) but none automatically implies AuthorizedAction: AI = Agent capable of producing governed artifacts, not AI = Authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Adversarial/objective-manipulation attacks rejected; objective versioning as a governance requirement
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 13: an AI intentionally recommends a_bad due to a misaligned objective; the decision policy's utility/constraint evaluation rejects it -- PASS. Notes a harder attack -- silently replacing the objective itself (e.g. MaximizeProfit -> MaximizeAgentReward) -- is not an ordinary decision error but a governance violation, requiring objectives that matter to be versioned and governed: an ObjectiveVersion with a decision's ObjectiveRef(D), enabling historical evaluation of D1 against O1. Experiment 14: D1 created under O1, O2 later activated; historical ObjectiveRef(D1)=O1 is retained -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Multi-objective weighted utility as a governance surface, never hidden in a prompt; unauthorized-weight-change rejection
b_rows_sample.statement: For multi-objective utility U = w1*U1 + w2*U2 + w3*U3 (e.g. cost/quality/risk), states the weights w_i are themselves governance choices: 'UtilityModel is part of decision governance when consequential. It should not be hidden inside an AI prompt.' Experiment 15: an AI changes w1 from 0.4 to 0.9 without authorization; the decision should reject the ungoverned utility model -- PASS, illustrating a deeper form of AI governance: governing not only AI output but also the DecisionModel and Objective.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision reproducibility bounded by computational-dependency reproducibility; missing model version rejected
b_rows_sample.statement: States DecisionReplay should reproduce a decision given K_t,O,C,P,M,D_R when deterministic semantics apply; for stochastic (AI/Monte Carlo) models, exact reproducibility may require RandomSeed and ModelVersion, and where exact reproduction is impossible the system should preserve relevant computational metadata (ModelId, ModelVersion, Prompt/ConfigurationRef, InputSnapshot, ComputationStatus). Gives the principle: a consequential decision should be reproducible to the extent its computational dependencies are reproducible. Experiment 16: a decision referencing Model=M with no version becomes ambiguous once the model changes, so it should be rejected or marked non-reproducible per policy -- PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Decision sensitivity/local robustness analysis; DecisionRobustness more informative than DecisionConfidence
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes DecisionConfidence alone is insufficient; proposes DecisionRobustness/sensitivity analysis. Example: a1 optimal for P(p)>0.55, a2 optimal below; at P(p)=0.56 the decision is highly sensitive (SensitivityHigh). Defines local robustness: D(K)=a is robust if D(K')=a for all K' in a neighborhood N(K). Experiment 17: a small perturbation P(p): 0.56->0.54 flips a1->a2, so the system records high sensitivity -- PASS. Notes this is more useful for human governance than a bare confidence percentage: 'A is selected under the current model, but the decision is highly sensitive to a small change in the relevant assumption.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: OutcomeQuality != DecisionQuality; decision calibration across many decisions
b_rows_sample.statement: Restates BadOutcome ⇏ BadDecision: a rational decision (e.g. P(success)=0.9) can still produce a bad outcome, so OutcomeQuality != DecisionQuality. Over many decisions D1,...,Dn, ExpectedUtility can be compared against RealizedUtility for empirical feedback, and DecisionCalibration becomes possible (e.g. among decisions predicted P(success)=0.8, ~80% should succeed if calibrated) -- 'calibration again'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Four new invariants: I_DecisionAuthority, I_DecisionBasis, I_ActionBoundary, I_ObjectiveIntegrity
b_rows_sample.statement: Adds four named invariants: I_DecisionAuthority (knowledge alone cannot authorize an action); I_DecisionBasis (every consequential decision references the knowledge, policy, objective, and computational basis required by its domain); I_ActionBoundary (decision selection does not imply execution); I_ObjectiveIntegrity (consequential decision objectives cannot be silently modified by an ungoverned agent).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 62 verdict: decision-making as its own bounded semantic layer; five-layer synthesis; opens Step 63 on causal reasoning/intervention
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 62 -- PASS with the refinement that KnowledgeOS must treat decision-making as its own bounded semantic layer between knowledge and authorization. Synthesizes five layers (Knowledge, Objective, DecisionPolicy, Authorization, Action) and the chain K + Objective + Constraints + Risk + Policy -> Decision -> (+ Authority + CurrentGovernance) -> Authorization -> (+ ExecutionPolicy) -> Action -> Outcome. Updates the running pipeline to Observation -> Evidence -> Knowledge -> Information -> Decision -> Authorization -> Action -> Outcome -> Learning. Opens Step 63 (Causal Reasoning and Intervention): distinguishing P(Y|X) from P(Y|do(X)) as 'absolutely central for KnowledgeOS' since a model may correctly learn P(Y|X) while still making the wrong decision about do(X) -- to investigate causal graphs, interventions, counterfactuals, treatment effects, confounding, mediation, causal evidence, causal assumptions, and the prediction/intervention boundary, framed as testing whether KnowledgeOS is a governed computational knowledge-and-decision system rather than merely an AI knowledge repository.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Structured CausalEstimate object with mandatory fully-specified Estimand; effect heterogeneity; CausalEffect != DecisionUtility
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines CE=(Treatment,Outcome,Estimand,Population,Method,Assumptions,Data,ModelVersion,Estimate,Uncertainty) as a structured causal result object. Requires Estimand to be fully specified (on whom, over what time, under what intervention, measured how, average or subgroup effect) -- 'effect of X on Y is incomplete'. Restates causal effect heterogeneity (ATE=0.2 can hide ATE_groupA=0.8 vs ATE_groupB=-0.1, so AverageEffect≠UniversalEffect, requiring Population scope preservation) and CausalEffect≠DecisionUtility (a positive effect can still yield negative net utility once cost is included), and reiterates temporal precedence alone is insufficient for causal direction (TemporalPrecedence ⇏ Causality).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Probability != Decision (identical success probability, different stakes yield different rational actions); Utility != Evidence; decision function D:(K,C,P,U,R)
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: P(Success|A)=0.8 identical across Case A (+100/-10) and Case B (+10/-1000) yields very different rational decisions -- Probability != Decision. Re-derives expected utility EU(A)=sum P(O_i|do(A))U(O_i); experiment 1 computes EU(A)=76 correctly. States utility is a preference/objective, not an empirical property -- Utility != Evidence; experiment 2 rejects inferring P(A)=High from U(A)=100. Defines the decision function D:(K,C,P,U,R) -> Decision (knowledge, context, policy, utility, risk constraints), 'considerably more accurate than AI->Decision'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Optimization within the feasible policy space; Decision != Authorization re-confirmed (experiments 3-4)
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: EU(A)=90>EU(B)=70 but Policy(A)=Forbidden correctly yields Decision=B -- PASS, confirming optimization occurs inside the feasible policy space (A*=argmax over A_allowed). Experiment 4: KnowledgeOS determining A*=Deploy while the executing agent lacks deployment authority correctly yields Decision=ApprovedPreference but Authorization=Denied -- PASS, reconfirming Decision != Authorization as 'one of our most important architectural boundaries'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Risk = Probability×Consequence approximation; catastrophic-low-probability rejection; hard constraint vs preference re-derived
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives Risk = Probability x Consequence as a basic approximation (real models may add exposure, uncertainty, detectability, reversibility, systemic effects). Experiment 5: P=0.001, Loss=-100M, policy forbidding catastrophic risk correctly yields ActionRejected despite low expected loss -- PASS. Re-derives hard constraint (A not-in A_allowed, eliminates alternatives) versus preference (U(A)>U(B), ranks them); experiment 6: two legally permissible actions with U(A)>U(B) yields A preferred but not mandatory -- PASS. Formalizes decision as constrained optimization: max_a U(a) subject to C_1(a),...,C_n(a)=True.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceConflict != ValueConflict; stakeholder utility disagreement is not disguised as a factual conflict
b_rows_sample.statement: Notes utility itself may be uncertain/contested: different stakeholders may assign U_A(a)!=U_B(a), so there may be no single objectively correct decision without specifying whose utility applies. Experiment 7: stakeholder A preferring A and stakeholder B preferring B, both legitimate under their declared objectives, correctly yields PreferenceConflict -- PASS, 'should not disguise a value conflict as a factual conflict'. States EvidenceConflict != ValueConflict ('Action A is likely to save 1M' is epistemic; 'saving 1M justifies this risk' is a value/policy question). Experiment 8: strong evidence for A rejected by stakeholders on ethical-cost grounds correctly yields KnowledgeSupports(A) while DecisionRejects(A) -- PASS, 'exactly how the architecture should behave'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Robust worst-case decision-making under interval-valued probability; distributional model uncertainty preserved
b_rows_sample.statement: For P(Success) in [0.6,0.9] (rather than a point estimate), a robust decision may consider the worst case min_{p in [0.6,0.9]} EU(A,p). Experiment 9: a probability interval correctly yields a decision based on a declared robust/risk policy rather than pretending P=0.8 is exact -- PASS. Notes E[X]=10 with unknown full distribution P(X) makes risk calculations sensitive to distributional assumptions, which KnowledgeOS should preserve. Experiment 10: two models (normality vs heavy tails) fitting data reasonably well but giving substantially different risk estimates correctly keeps ModelUncertainty visible -- PASS.

b_aliases: Step 62 Decision Theory and Knowledge-to-Action Boundary

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'kos-decision-theory-model' POSSIBLY relates to 'decision-contract-admissibility-model' (batch B0023). Note: Step 62's decision-theoretic layer: the decision problem tuple, expected utility with non-universal decision-rule caveat, hard-constraint-vs-preference, risk-sensitive/robust (minimax) policies, aleatoric-vs-epistemic uncertainty, EVSI-governed information acquisition, Selected≠Authorized, objective/utility-weight governance, decision reproducibility, sensitivity/robustness analysis, and outcome-vs-decision-quality calibration; four new named invariants (I_DecisionAuthority, I_DecisionBasis, I_ActionBoundary, I_ObjectiveIntegrity). Builds directly on decision-contract-admissibility-model (Step 42) and decision-experiment-object (VOI, earlier batch).

a_rows_sample.anchor: How do we ensure that a KnowledgeOS decision gate can never authorize a state that violates a mandatory invariant?
a_rows_sample.statement: Three distinct questions must be separated: Question 1 (Epistemic) 'Do we have sufficient knowledge?'; Question 2 (Logical) 'Are the decision conditions internally consistent?'; Question 3 (Governance/safety) 'Is the resulting action permitted?'. Therefore SufficientKnowledge != ValidDecision != AuthorizedAction. This distinction is stated as fundamental, moving the investigation from 'do we know enough' to 'is the decision formally admissible'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: DC(d)=(Pre,Inv,Auth,Post,Temporal,Evidence)
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a first-version Decision Contract DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Post, Temporal, Evidence): preconditions (what must already be true, e.g. IdentityConfirmed=True), invariants (what must never be violated, e.g. ProductionChange=>Approved, VoteCount<=MaximumAllowed, explicitly a domain constraint not merely evidence), authorization requirements, required postconditions, timing constraints, and assurance requirements. Preconditions and invariants are kept strictly separate: a precondition asks whether the world is ready for the operation; an invariant asks whether the operation is allowed to produce a state violating a protected property.

a_rows_sample.anchor: {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}
a_rows_sample.statement: Borrows Hoare-logic style {P} d {Q} (if precondition P holds, execution of d should produce a state satisfying Q) and applies it as {Pre(d)} d {Post(d)}. Immediately argues ordinary Hoare logic is insufficient for KnowledgeOS because it additionally needs Evidence, Uncertainty, Authority, TemporalValidity and Provenance -- so the KnowledgeOS decision contract must extend the classical Hoare form.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Admissible = Pre and Invariant and Assurance and Authorization
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Admissible(d,K,t) iff Pre(d,K,t) and Invariant(d,K,t) and Assurance(d,K,t) and Authorization(d,K,t) -- a strict conjunction. Worked example: if Pre=True, Assurance=True, Authorization=True but Invariant=False, then Admissible=False regardless; 'there must be no averaging' across the conjuncts (i.e. no compensable weighted-sum scoring of admissibility conditions).

a_rows_sample.anchor: DC(d)=<P,I,A,E,Q,T,O>; Admissible as six-way conjunction
a_rows_sample.statement: Restates and extends the Decision Contract as DC(d) = <P,I,A,E,Q,T,O> where P=preconditions, I=invariants, A=authorization, E=evidence requirements, Q=epistemic sufficiency, T=temporal constraints, O=postconditions; and Admissible(d,K,t) iff P(K,t) and I(K,t) and A(K,t) and E(K,t) and Q(K,t) and T(K,t), with Execute(d) only then permitted.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Decision evaluation != decision execution; dry-run capability
a_rows_sample.statement: States that KnowledgeOS should conceptually perform Evaluate(d) before Execute(d), so Decision evaluation != Decision execution. The architecture should support Evaluate(d,K) without actually executing d, enabling simulation, review, what-if analysis, governance checks and AI planning; extends to a counterfactual decision WhatIf(Execute(d)) with estimated PostState(d), flagged as important for the later causal-reasoning formalization.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Safety gate pipeline: Plan->Evaluate->Validate->Authorize->Safety Gate->Execute->Observe Outcome
a_rows_sample.statement: For consequential operations, depicts a pipeline Plan -> Evaluate -> Validate -> Authorize -> Safety Gate -> Execute -> Observe Outcome, with the rule that the side effect must occur after the gate. Applies this to bound AI agents: an AI agent may propose d but should not automatically bypass Admissibility, so AIProposal -> DecisionEvaluation -> PolicyGate; states the architecture rule 'AI may propose; the governed system decides whether the proposal is admissible', and explicitly rejects Trust(AI)=True in favor of Capability(AI) constrained by Policy -- an AI agent's authority is explicitly bounded.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 42 (all PASS)
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests against the Step 42 model, all recorded PASS: (1) epistemic requirements pass but authorization fails => Admissible=False; (2) authorization passes but a hard invariant fails => Block; (3) all conditions known except a safety-critical invariant => Block/Unknown per policy, never automatic authorization; (4) a valid transition from a valid state preserves the invariant; (5) a transition that would violate a domain invariant is rejected; (6) a required approval expires before execution => decision becomes inadmissible; (7) evidence used by a decision is revoked => dependency closure identifies affected assurance and decisions; (8) an AI proposes an action violating a governance rule => proposal may be recorded but execution is blocked; (9) new evidence disproves an earlier assumption => existing assurance can be downgraded/revoked; (10) a decision is evaluated without execution => dry-run result has no side effect; (11) an invariant belongs to bounded context BC_A => KnowledgeOS does not silently redefine it from BC_B; (12) a decision passes technical assurance but lacks governance authorization => TechnicallySupported=True, Authorized=False, therefore Execute=False.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Step 42 verdict and seven closing principles
a_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 42 -- PASS and restates seven principles as the step's headline results: (1) Sufficient Knowledge != Valid Decision; (2) Valid Decision != Authorized Action; (3) Unknown safety state must not silently become safe; (4) Hard invariants are non-negotiable; (5) AI proposal != authorized execution; (6) Every consequential decision should have an explicit contract; (7) Evidence invalidation must propagate through decision dependencies.

a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the Step 42 decision contract to DC(d) = (Pre, Inv, Auth, Evidence, Post, Effects), where Effects(A) = {E_1,...,E_n} covers both ExpectedEffect and PotentialSideEffects, so the system should evaluate not only the immediate postcondition but what important downstream states an action could create. Defines horizon-dependent reachability safety: an action A is safe only if Reach_H(S,A) intersect S_unsafe = empty for horizon H -- safety cannot usually be proven for t->infinity, so a finite horizon (e.g. 24h or 30 days) must be chosen, making Safety(d,H) horizon-specific (an action safe for H=1 day may be unsafe for H=2 years). Some actions have Lag(A,Y)>0 (e.g. ArchitectureChange -> MaintenanceCost manifesting months later); represents delayed causality as Y_{t+tau}=f(A_t,...) with delay tau as part of the causal model; warns that a controller reacting before a previous action's effects become visible (A_t -> S_{t+tau} -> Decision_{t+tau+1}) can overcorrect, producing oscillation (Increase->Decrease->Increase->Decrease) even when each local decision appears rational -- 'the problem lies in the dynamic system', so the decision engine should consider EffectDelay, not merely EffectExists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Gate(d,K,t)=InvariantSatisfied(d,K,t); Unknown safety condition != Safe
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a safety gate as Gate(d,K,t)=InvariantSatisfied(d,K,t), with the rule that for critical invariants False => Block. For the case Invariant=Unknown, argues the default should generally be Block for safety-critical decisions -- 'a very strong architectural default' framed as a policy decision, formalized as Unknown safety condition != Safe.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Open-world versus closed-world interpretation
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes open-world semantics (absence of evidence for A does not imply not-A) from closed-world semantics (system may treat unknown A as False). Argues KnowledgeOS should not adopt one universal assumption; the applicable domain policy must specify which semantics apply. For a safety gate, Unknown->Block is usually appropriate; for exploratory analytics, Unknown->ContinueWithWarning may be appropriate; Policy_decision determines the treatment of unknowns.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Invariant taxonomy: structural, temporal, numerical, referential, governance, security
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes six invariant kinds with examples: Structural (Entity must have exactly one owner), Temporal (Approval must precede deployment), Numerical (Amount>=0), Referential (EveryClaim -> ValidEvidence), Governance (ProductionChange -> RequiredApproval), Security (Credential must not be exposed).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Invariant ownership and DDD aggregate boundaries
b_rows_sample.statement: In DDD, invariants often belong to an aggregate boundary (Aggregate must guarantee Invariant(AggregateState)); KnowledgeOS should respect that ownership and not arbitrarily redefine an aggregate's invariants. Every invariant should have an OwnerContext (e.g. Invariant_1 -> BC_Voting, Invariant_2 -> BC_Governance). This prevents KnowledgeOS from becoming the owner of every business invariant: instead KnowledgeOS represents, evaluates and traces governed invariants while the domain remains authoritative.

b_rows_sample.anchor: HardInvariant versus PolicyConstraint versus AdvisoryCondition
b_rows_sample.statement: First proposes InvariantType in {Hard, Soft, Advisory} (Hard: violation blocks action; Soft: violation requires explicit justification; Advisory: violation produces warning), then self-corrects: strictly speaking a property that CAN be violated is not an invariant in the mathematical sense, so the vocabulary should instead be HardInvariant versus PolicyConstraint versus AdvisoryCondition -- flagged explicitly as 'a useful correction in our formal vocabulary'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Formal invariant I(s)=True over reachable states; inductive invariant reasoning
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a true invariant as I(s)=True for every reachable valid state s, established inductively: base case I(s_0)=True, inductive step I(s) and ValidTransition(s,s') => I(s'), concluding I holds for all reachable states -- noted as powerful for software verification. Applies it to a governed workflow Requested->Reviewed->Approved->Provisioned with the invariant Provisioned=>Approved, requiring it be impossible for a valid transition to produce Provisioned & not-Approved.

b_rows_sample.anchor: State transition system S, T subset SxS, safety requirement
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines S as the set of system states, T subset of SxS as valid transitions, and an invariant I:S->{True,False}; the safety requirement is (s,s') in T and I(s) => I(s'). Connects this directly to event-driven architecture: an event such as ApprovalGranted must follow the domain's event semantics, and KnowledgeOS can reconstruct State_t from Events_<=t -- but an event itself may be invalid, so EventValid(e,K,t) must be checked (an invalid event must not silently establish a valid state). Each state transition should ideally be traceable end to end: Event -> Actor -> Evidence -> Authorization, giving complete decision lineage.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Temporal invariant and temporal validity window
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes ordering invariants as t_approval < t_deployment (violated if t_deployment <= t_approval), and separately temporal validity: a fact can be true but stale -- e.g. SecurityApproved(t_1) is used at decision time t_2, requiring t_2 in ValidityWindow(SecurityApproval). Composes multiple temporal conditions into TemporalSufficiency(d,t) = ApprovalValid(t) and SecurityValid(t) and TestValid(t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Twelve falsification experiments for Step 42 (all PASS)
b_rows_sample.statement: Runs twelve falsification tests against the Step 42 model, all recorded PASS: (1) epistemic requirements pass but authorization fails => Admissible=False; (2) authorization passes but a hard invariant fails => Block; (3) all conditions known except a safety-critical invariant => Block/Unknown per policy, never automatic authorization; (4) a valid transition from a valid state preserves the invariant; (5) a transition that would violate a domain invariant is rejected; (6) a required approval expires before execution => decision becomes inadmissible; (7) evidence used by a decision is revoked => dependency closure identifies affected assurance and decisions; (8) an AI proposes an action violating a governance rule => proposal may be recorded but execution is blocked; (9) new evidence disproves an earlier assumption => existing assurance can be downgraded/revoked; (10) a decision is evaluated without execution => dry-run result has no side effect; (11) an invariant belongs to bounded context BC_A => KnowledgeOS does not silently redefine it from BC_B; (12) a decision passes technical assurance but lacks governance authorization => TechnicallySupported=True, Authorized=False, therefore Execute=False.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 42 verdict and seven closing principles
b_rows_sample.statement: Declares STEP 42 -- PASS and restates seven principles as the step's headline results: (1) Sufficient Knowledge != Valid Decision; (2) Valid Decision != Authorized Action; (3) Unknown safety state must not silently become safe; (4) Hard invariants are non-negotiable; (5) AI proposal != authorized execution; (6) Every consequential decision should have an explicit contract; (7) Evidence invalidation must propagate through decision dependencies.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: Purification = Dimension Expansion + Dimension Refinement
a_rows_sample.statement: Purification(K_t)->K_{t+1} should not mean simply adding more knowledge; it means transforming a knowledge state to become richer in relevant dimensions and more qualified/coherent/reliable/discriminating along them. Formalized as Dimension Expansion (D_t subset D_{t+1}, discovering/incorporating additional relevant dimensions) plus Dimension Refinement (for existing dimension d, v_t(d) -> v_{t+1}(d), quality/value along that dimension increases). Knowledge state reconceived as K_t=(D_t,V_t,R_t,P_t,...) rather than a set of facts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Every purification dimension requires an explicit ordering or transformation semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Cannot assume v_{t+1} > v_t is always improvement ('higher is not always better'): e.g. uncertainty may decrease, provenance completeness may increase, contradiction may decrease, evidence quality/relevance/confidence may increase, but raw information quantity could increase while epistemic quality decreases. Each dimension d needs its own order relation preceq_d, with v_t(d) preceq_d v_{t+1}(d) meaning improvement per that dimension's declared ordering. Connects directly to the unresolved Step 287 issue that not every Sigma axis has a natural order (Acquisition A flagged as already problematic); states as a research requirement that every purification dimension requires an explicit ordering or transformation semantics.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E_d(K_t)=K_{t+1} ... R_d(K_t)=K_{t+1} ... C(K_t,o)=K_{t+1} ... X(K_t)\rightarrow \text{conflict-qualified state} ... Z(K_t)\rightarrow G_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Six candidate (not canonical) operators: E (Expansion) discovers a new relevant dimension d not-in D_t, now in D_{t+1}; R_d (Refinement) improves an existing dimension, v_t(d) prec_d v_{t+1}(d); C (Correction) changes an existing value because new evidence shows the previous state was wrong -- explicitly Purification != monotonic accumulation, since a purified state may contain less due to removed erroneous knowledge; X (Contradiction resolution) given p and not-p, the kernel must not arbitrarily select one, producing a conflict-qualified state until Buddhi/evidence/qualification can discriminate; Q (Qualification), the unresolved G1 operator, determining sufficient justification for the intended epistemic purpose, reframed via the recent Cavell-derived reconsideration so purification can mean correctly recognizing a gap cannot currently be resolved rather than resolving it; Z (Zero detection) detects epistemic absence, Z(K_t)->G_t (recognized gaps), with G_t transformable via E,R,C,Q into G_{t+1} -- the system becomes more purified partly by knowing more accurately what it does not know.

a_rows_sample.anchor: E\circ Q \neq Q\circ E ... This is potentially a non-commutative epistemic algebra.
a_rows_sample.statement: Buddhi reframed as an operator-selection mechanism B(K_t,O_t)->which transformation (from {E,R,C,X,Q,Z,...}) is appropriate, rather than another knowledge dimension -- 'the Kernel is not merely storing knowledge, it continuously discriminates what epistemic operation should happen next'. Yoga reframed as operator composition Y = O_n o ... o O_1, e.g. Y_purify = Q o C o R o E o Z (detect absence -> discover dimension -> refine/correct -> qualify -> new state) vs Y_conflict = Q o X o C. Proposes studying the resulting algebra's closure, associativity, and (expected) non-commutativity, e.g. E o Q != Q o E because discovering a dimension before qualification differs from qualifying before discovering it -- hypothesized as a non-commutative epistemic algebra.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Moksha = \lim_{t\rightarrow T} \operatorname{Purify}(K_t)
a_rows_sample.statement: Purification should be modelled as a partially ordered trajectory K_0->K_1->...->K_n (respecting Step 287's product-order finding), not a scalar purity score P(K_t); K_2 may be better than K_1 in some dimensions but incomparable in others. Purification defined formally as K_t->K_{t+1} when the transformation increases epistemic adequacy via D_{t+1} superset-or-equal D_t and/or for-all d in D_t, v_t(d) preceq_d v_{t+1}(d), while allowing correction (false(p)->removed/reclassified) and qualification (unknown->explicitly unknown) -- so purification is epistemic-adequacy-monotonic under an appropriate partial order, not information-monotonic. Correspondingly rejects Moksha=max(K); proposes instead Moksha = lim_{t->T} Purify(K_t), where the limit might mean dimensional completeness relative to a declared horizon, maximal epistemic qualification, minimal unresolved error, maximal justified value across relevant dimensions, or a change of epistemic regime -- explicitly leaving well-definedness of this limit to mathematics, not philosophy, to determine.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic Purification Algebra ... five questions
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes structuring the next mathematical investigation as an 'Epistemic Purification Algebra' research programme with five questions: (1) what exactly is a knowledge dimension, (2) what does 'value' mean for each dimension, (3) which operators transform dimensions and values, (4) what algebraic laws govern composition of those operators, (5) does repeated purification converge toward a meaningful epistemic limit -- only after answering these should Moksha's formal role be assessed. Envisions KnowledgeOS Kernel = Mind becoming computationally interpretable: Buddhi chooses epistemic operators, Yoga composes them, purification is the resulting trajectory through multidimensional Knowledge State space.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sentence \rightarrow \text{proposition about a dimension} ... Sentence can instantiate a knowledge dimension
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects sentence=dimension; a sentence should instead be treated as a proposition about a dimension, which under certain conditions instantiates a knowledge dimension. Worked example: 'Water boils at 100C at standard atmospheric pressure' does not itself define the dimension d=boiling point of water under specified pressure; rather the sentence supplies a value v(d)=100C, giving Dimension d + Value v + Context c.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Sentence \neq \text{Proposition} \neq \text{Dimension}
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Sentence != Proposition != Dimension via example: sentence s='Buddhi distinguishes' -> proposition p='Buddhi performs discrimination' -> dimension d='discrimination capability' -> value v(d) in {high,low,unknown} or later v(d) in [0,1]; a second sentence ('Buddhi should distinguish the permanent from the impermanent') can modify the same dimension d, so many sentences can contribute to one dimension. Prescribes a disciplined pipeline: Sentence -> Proposition -> Semantic interpretation -> Candidate dimension -> Dimension definition -> Evidence/context -> Value, to keep the Gita programme scientifically disciplined (a dimension must not be chosen merely because it sounds philosophically appropriate).

a_rows_sample.anchor: \text{Sentence addition} \rightarrow \begin{cases}\text{new dimension}\\\text{new value}\\\text{new context}\\\text{new relation}\\\text{correction}\\\text{qualification}\end{cases}
a_rows_sample.statement: Reframes the purification model: adding a new sentence's important effect is often D_1>D_0 (a new dimension is discovered) rather than |K_1|>|K_0| (more propositions), and further evidence can separately improve the value of an existing dimension v_0(d)->v_1(d); yields a small operator taxonomy that sentence addition maps to: new dimension, new value, new context, new relation, correction, or qualification -- described as exactly the operator algebra sought.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "One sentence may reveal or instantiate one or more knowledge dimensions." a **research hypothesis**, not a canonical rule
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes as a testable, falsifiable research hypothesis (not canonical rule): 'one sentence may reveal or instantiate one or more knowledge dimensions'; recommends testing it against a substantial corpus of Gita statements and ordinary KnowledgeOS knowledge -- if the same sentence routinely contains multiple independent dimensions, this falsifies a simplistic one-sentence/one-dimension model, and the experiment could lead to a rigorous Knowledge Atom -> Dimension -> Value -> Purification Operator definition chain.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1} \succeq_{Pareto} K_t \iff \forall d:\ v_{t+1}(d) \text{ no worse} \ \wedge\ \exists d:\ \text{strictly better}
a_rows_sample.statement: S2226's refusal of v_{t+1}>v_t ('higher is not always better': uncertainty may decrease, provenance completeness may increase, contradiction may decrease) is formally a Pareto-dominance problem: K_{t+1} succeq_Pareto K_t iff for all dimensions d, v_{t+1}(d) is no worse, and for some d, strictly better -- a Pareto order is a partial order admitting incomparable states by construction. Identified as the FIFTH independent route (of five distinct methods: Sigma-axis-order measurement per Step 291 finding 0 of 5 axes ordered; retraction non-monotonicity per Step 288/06; two separate corpus refusals to claim a semilattice, Steps 060 sec60.71 and 061/274.32; and now this Pareto argument) all converging on: there is no total order on K -- assessed as among the best-supported negative results in the programme.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Moksha \sim transcendence of the conditioning regime ... G_t\rightarrow G_{\perp}
a_rows_sample.statement: Revises the earlier Moksha formulation (Delta_t -> 0) given Chapter 14: Moksha != maximum K and Moksha != maximum Sattva; instead Moksha ~ transcendence of the conditioning regime, formalized as the research placeholder G_t -> G_perp meaning 'outside the three-mode conditioning model' -- explicitly flagged as a KnowledgeOS mathematical placeholder, not a Gita term. Proposes a purification trajectory Tamas-dominant -> (discrimination/clarification) -> Rajas-dominant -> (disciplined activity) -> Sattva-dominant -> (transcendence) -> Guna-atita, and a candidate epistemic-state model E_t=(K_t,Sigma_t,G_t,N_t) with N_t -Buddhi-> o_t and K_{t+1}=delta(K_t,o_t).

a_rows_sample.anchor: \Delta\text{Knowledge} = \Delta\text{Dimension} + \Delta\text{Quality} ... Knowledge Growth requires Discrimination
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes dimension from value: a statement could add a new dimension but have poor epistemic quality, or add no new dimension yet dramatically improve reliability/consistency/provenance/resolution/confidence/contextual understanding -- decomposed (as a research decomposition only) as Delta Knowledge = Delta Dimension + Delta Quality. Argues K_{t+1}>K_t in quantity does not imply K_{t+1} succ K_t epistemically, because more information != better knowledge; the kernel therefore requires Buddhi to discriminate: Knowledge Growth requires Discrimination, not merely ingestion.

a_rows_sample.anchor: M\neq K_{\max} ... M\neq |\mathcal K|\rightarrow\infty ... M\sim\text{transformation of the relationship between Knower, Field and Horizon}
a_rows_sample.statement: With Chapters 11-14 combined, refuses modeling Moksha as the final Knowledge State: M != K_max and M != |K|->infinity. Proposes instead M ~ transformation of the relationship between Knower, Field and Horizon, combined with Chapter 14's transcendence of ordinary conditioning; the theoretical transition is not simply K_0->K_1->K_2->... but (N,K_t,rho_t,G_t,Omega) -> different epistemic regime.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge quantity \neq Knowledge quality ... Purification \neq accumulation
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines purification: P:Sigma_t->Sigma_{t+1} must not assume P(Sigma_t)>Sigma_t (per Step 287's finding that axes lack fully declared orders); instead a desired property Q(Sigma_{t+1})>=Q(Sigma_t) is wanted where Q is a future epistemic-quality functional that does not yet exist (an important research gap). Illustrates via example that K_1={1000 unsupported claims} could contain more information than K_2={100 well-supported claims} yet K_2 may be epistemically superior -- so Knowledge quantity != Knowledge quality, and Purification != accumulation; the kernel should maximize epistemic adequacy, not raw knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: confidence: 0.9\rightarrow0.4 could actually represent epistemic improvement ... Purification \neq monotonic increase of every metric
a_rows_sample.statement: Sharpens the non-monotonicity of purification with a concrete numeric example: confidence going from 0.9 to 0.4 could represent epistemic improvement if new evidence shows the previous certainty was unjustified. Hence Purification != monotonic increase of every metric; Purification = progress toward a better-qualified epistemic state. Proposes P(K_t,E_t,B_t)=K_{t+1} performing: remove unsupported claims, resolve contradictions, separate observation from interpretation, identify missing evidence, reduce unjustified certainty, preserve provenance, incorporate valid new evidence, identify new dimensions. Also defines a transformation-quality functional Q_B(K_t,K_{t+1}) assessing whether a transition reduces contradiction, reduces unsupported assertions, makes uncertainty explicit, improves provenance, increases justified knowledge, detects hidden gaps, or avoids introducing unsupported claims -- assessed as more promising than trying to mathematically encode 'good' and 'evil'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge growth ... Knowledge expansion ... Knowledge purification ... These are not equivalent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly rejects Purification=increase-in-dimensions-and-values as the canonical mathematical definition (confidence 0.95->0.55 can represent improvement if the original confidence was unjustified): Purification != monotonic increase; P(K_t,K_{t+1}) = improvement in epistemic quality, with quality itself still needing formal definition. Distinguishes three non-equivalent concepts: Knowledge growth (K_t->K_{t+1}, a state change occurs); Knowledge expansion (dim(K_{t+1})>dim(K_t), new dimensions represented); Knowledge purification (P(K_t,K_{t+1})=true, epistemic quality improves) -- more information does not imply better knowledge, and knowledge expansion != knowledge purification, assessed as an important theoretical safeguard. Also reformulates purification against Sigma as Sigma_t --B,Q,delta--> Sigma_{t+1} with P(Sigma_t,Sigma_{t+1}) rather than a scalar purity score, given Step 287's problem with total ordering.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Purification \approx reduction of epistemic distortion ... K_{t+1}\not\supseteq K_t does not imply deterioration.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects purification=increasing knowledge dimensions/values as the primary definition; proposes Purification ~ reduction of epistemic distortion, not more information. Example: K_t with P=verified becomes K_{t+1} with P=uncertain because new evidence shows the prior verification was inadequate -- numerically less certainty, epistemically better. Hence K_{t+1} not-superset-or-equal K_t does not imply deterioration.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Q(K_{t+1}) > Q(K_t) ... 100 pieces of noisy knowledge \downarrow purification \downarrow 20 pieces of highly qualified knowledge
a_rows_sample.statement: From 5.11 (purification through disciplined action without attachment): sharpens purification from |K_{t+1}|>|K_t| to Q(K_{t+1})>Q(K_t) where Q is a future epistemic-quality function. Concrete illustration: a kernel could transform 100 pieces of noisy knowledge into 20 pieces of highly qualified knowledge, becoming better despite becoming smaller -- assessed as a major correction to a purely information-quantity model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: J_t = w_A A_t+ w_S S_t+ w_R R_t+ w_V V_t+ w_C C_t - \lambda Z_t - \mu U_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes, explicitly non-canonical/for research purposes only, a candidate kernel objective function J_t = w_A A_t + w_S S_t + w_R R_t + w_V V_t + w_C C_t - lambda Z_t - mu U_t (weighted five Sigma axes minus unresolved-gap term Z minus unjustified-commitment term U), with purification meaning J_{t+1}>J_t -- explicitly not adopted because the measurement scales and per-axis ordering remain unresolved (per Step 287). Proposes Moksha as the limiting condition where repeated purification cycles reach Delta J -> 0 (the kernel can no longer improve the state under the available epistemic horizon) -- a philosophical hypothesis, not an architecture decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel = the smallest unit capable of epistemic state transition
b_rows_sample.statement: Central hypothesis: KnowledgeOS Kernel = the smallest unit capable of epistemic state transition, not merely the smallest unit that stores knowledge. Kernel = (State, Transition Capability): the state is what the kernel currently holds, the transition capability determines what can legitimately happen to that state. Gita lens (analytical, not DDD names): Mind -> evolving epistemic state, Buddhi -> discriminative capability, Karma -> action/transition, Phala -> resulting state/outcome.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K = (K_t,\Omega_K)
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate kernel K=(K_t,Omega_K) with 11 candidate operations, each carrying a load-bearing distinction: (1) Observe(O_t) with O_t != K_t (observation is not automatically knowledge, preserving W->O->E and Qualify); (2) Discriminate(K_t,O_t)->{d_1..d_n} = the Buddhi operation, meaning 'distinguish', not yet 'decide truth'; (3) Qualify(x,E,C,t,Pi), the G1 unresolved operation, whose result may be {admit,reject,defer,qualify} rather than binary {true,false}; (4) Incorporate: K_{t+1}=Incorporate(K_t,p), a state transformation not simple insertion; (5) Reject(K_t,p) with Reject != Prove False (a proposition can be rejected as insufficiently qualified without being established false); (6) Contradict: recognizing p _|_ q via the corpus's Relation primitive; (7) Revise(K_t,p,E) for evidence-conflicting knowledge, with explicit warning not to import AGM revision theory merely because it exists, per Step 287; (8) Supersede: p_1 supersedes p_2 while preserving lineage; (9) Recall(K_t,h)/Remember distinguishing currently-known from historically-known, with K_t != H_K (history of states/transitions); (10) Withdraw(p): K_t -> K_{t+1} with withdraw != delete history (the historical fact of having held it may remain, important for auditability); (11) Act/Transform(a), external to the epistemic state per Command != Transformation != Result and Step 285's finding that Action, Event, Policy were external to the verification projection.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \delta:(K_t,O_t,C_t)\rightarrow K_{t+1} ... only when the transition satisfies the kernel's invariants
b_rows_sample.statement: The kernel should not be an unrestricted machine: reject delta:KxO->K as an unrestricted transition function; instead delta:(K_t,O_t,C_t)->K_{t+1} only when the transition satisfies the kernel's invariants. Kernel operation = candidate transition + discrimination + qualification + state transition, subject to constraints. Motivated by the 'mind can become its own enemy' observation made mathematically useful.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \Omega_K = \{\operatorname{Discriminate},\operatorname{Qualify},\operatorname{Transition}\}
b_rows_sample.statement: Speculative minimal-algebra hypothesis: Omega_K = {Discriminate, Qualify, Transition} might suffice, with Accept/Reject/Revise/Supersede as specialized transition types -- explicitly flagged 'we should not assume this minimality', proposed as a mathematical question to attack rather than an established result.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel: the smallest bounded epistemic mechanism that maintains a time-indexed knowledge state and can discriminate and perform legitimate transitions of that state under the applicable constraints.
b_rows_sample.statement: Provisional formal kernel definition: K = (K_t, Omega_K, I) where K_t = current knowledge state, Omega_K = permitted kernel operations, I = kernel invariants; K_t --omega in Omega_K--> K_{t+1} only if I(K_t,omega,K_{t+1})=true. Gita gives only the philosophical lens Mind~Kernel, Buddhi~discriminative capability; the mathematical/DDD investigation determines the actual kernel. Key research hypothesis: Kernel != Knowledge Store, but potentially Kernel = Epistemic State + Discrimination + Legitimate State Transition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 291 — KnowledgeOS Kernel and Operation Algebra
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes next research step 'Step 291 -- KnowledgeOS Kernel and Operation Algebra' with 12 questions: minimal kernel definition; whether K_t is the kernel state or the kernel holds additional state; minimal Omega_K; which operations are genuinely epistemic vs belong outside (Governance, Authority, Action, Replay); whether Discriminate is primitive or composite; what Qualify consumes/produces; whether every legitimate K_t->K_{t+1} transition can be classified; determinism of the transition; which invariants must never be violated; whether the operation algebra can be proven minimal; which parts are independently derivable vs merely Gita-correspondences.

b_rows_sample.anchor: B(K_t,x)\rightarrow d ... d \in \{\text{supported},\text{refuted},\text{contradictory},\text{unknown},\text{unqualified},\text{inadmissible}\}
b_rows_sample.statement: Mathematical correction to 'the kernel should always be busy determining right and wrong': right/wrong should not initially be binary. Buddhi should implement a discrimination function B(K_t,x) -> d with d in {supported, refuted, contradictory, unknown, unqualified, inadmissible}, not a Boolean truth oracle. Hence Buddhi = epistemic discrimination, not Buddhi = truth; the kernel does not create truth, it evaluates what can legitimately be concluded from its current state and evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal B: (K_t,O_t,E_t,C_t) \rightarrow D_t
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes B:(K_t,O_t,E_t,C_t)->D_t (discrimination/decision result), enumerating what B must do: distinguish, compare, validate, detect contradiction, assess evidence, qualify, reject, accept, defer, update the knowledge state, preserve provenance, determine what remains unknown. Central hypothesis: KnowledgeOS Kernel ~philosophically~ Mind; Buddhi ~philosophically~ Kernel's discrimination capability; K_t = changing Knowledge State; K (calligraphic) = Knowledge Space. Four-level picture: Knowledge Space K -> Knowledge State K_t -> KnowledgeOS Kernel -> Buddhi -> epistemic operations -> K_{t+1}. Explicitly marked as hypothesis pending testing against actual Gita passages and the existing KnowledgeOS corpus, not yet canonical.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal K \overset{\Omega}{\longrightarrow} O_t \overset{\mathcal B}{\longrightarrow} D_t \overset{\delta}{\longrightarrow} K_{t+1}
b_rows_sample.statement: The central kernel question evolves from 'what operations does the Kernel perform?' to 'what can a bounded KnowledgeOS Kernel legitimately know, observe, discriminate, and conclude about a knowledge space larger than its current state?'. Final research-model pipeline: K (Knowledge Space) --Omega (observation/projection)--> O_t (observation) --B (Buddhi/discrimination)--> D_t (discrimination result) --delta (state transition)--> K_{t+1} (new Knowledge State). Explicitly not yet canonical architecture; identifies convergence of existing open questions about Observation, Proposition, State, Event, Buddhi, Qualify, delta, and the five-axis Sigma.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can the existing KnowledgeOS eight primitives and the five-axis \Sigma=(A,S,R,V,C) express the proposed Mind–Buddhi–Kernel behavior without introducing a new primitive?
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes pausing philosophical interpretation after Chapter 12 to test mathematically: can the existing eight primitives and five-axis Sigma=(A,S,R,V,C) express the proposed Mind-Buddhi-Kernel behavior without a new primitive? Specifically test whether Buddhi = an operation over existing primitives, Mind = a state/orientation over existing primitives, and Kernel = (K_t, operations, invariants, transition rules) -- framed as the first real mathematical/DDD test of the 'KnowledgeOS Kernel = Mind' interpretation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: E_d(K_t)=K_{t+1} ... R_d(K_t)=K_{t+1} ... C(K_t,o)=K_{t+1} ... X(K_t)\rightarrow \text{conflict-qualified state} ... Z(K_t)\rightarrow G_t
b_rows_sample.statement: Six candidate (not canonical) operators: E (Expansion) discovers a new relevant dimension d not-in D_t, now in D_{t+1}; R_d (Refinement) improves an existing dimension, v_t(d) prec_d v_{t+1}(d); C (Correction) changes an existing value because new evidence shows the previous state was wrong -- explicitly Purification != monotonic accumulation, since a purified state may contain less due to removed erroneous knowledge; X (Contradiction resolution) given p and not-p, the kernel must not arbitrarily select one, producing a conflict-qualified state until Buddhi/evidence/qualification can discriminate; Q (Qualification), the unresolved G1 operator, determining sufficient justification for the intended epistemic purpose, reframed via the recent Cavell-derived reconsideration so purification can mean correctly recognizing a gap cannot currently be resolved rather than resolving it; Z (Zero detection) detects epistemic absence, Z(K_t)->G_t (recognized gaps), with G_t transformable via E,R,C,Q into G_{t+1} -- the system becomes more purified partly by knowing more accurately what it does not know.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \{\operatorname{Discriminate},\ \operatorname{Qualify},\ \operatorname{Transition}\}\ \cong\ \{\equiv,\ G1,\ \delta\}
b_rows_sample.statement: The philosophically-proposed minimal kernel algebra Omega_K={Discriminate,Qualify,Transition} (from S2219, the kernel-definition-from-evidence-maths-DDD file) maps exactly onto the formal lane's independently-established blockers: Discriminate = the equality/distinguishability relation equiv (the unique minimal cycle cut per Steps 289/291, unique over both graph universes); Qualify = the corpus's own Qualify:Observation x Policy -> Evidence, i.e. G1, named/typed/no body, irreducible; Transition = K_t --delta--> K_{t+1}, i.e. delta, commit case unspecifiable, executed as K1 is K0. This is a genuine independent arrival (derived from 'what must a kernel be able to do', not from the dependency graph, 261.23, or the G1 register) but a NEGATIVE convergence: it solves none of the three, and is a restatement of the blocker set, not a kernel. Registered as new gap G-90 (derived, raises confidence, closes nothing). Sharp consequence stated: any minimal kernel algebra containing Qualify inherits G1 -- since Qualify is the one irreducible gap, a genuinely minimal kernel cannot be closed without closing G1.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A correctly shaped triple whose three components are EXACTLY the three open items. It states the problem well. It populates nothing.
b_rows_sample.statement: Tests the proposed kernel shape K=(K_t,Omega_K,I) slot by slot against the formal lane: K_t (the state) is OPEN (per Step 285; 258.35 says it may not be a tuple at all); Omega_K (permitted operations) is OPEN (N-4 mandatory membership open, 0 of 22 operations has a body/identity/ratification per 291); I (invariants) has 0 of 7 established (per REFINED-STEP-287-INVARIANTS), and I is downstream of equiv in 261.30's chain. Conclusion: a correctly-shaped triple whose three components are exactly the three open items -- a well-posed problem statement, not progress toward closure; must not be mistaken for populating the kernel (per 291's 'shape -> content requires a derivation, and none exists').

b_rows_sample.anchor: 1. Perceive / receive ... 5. Orient
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the KnowledgeOS kernel may need five fundamentally different classes of work: (1) Perceive/receive O_t; (2) Represent O_t->K_t; (3) Discriminate B_t(K_t,O_t)->d_t; (4) Transform delta(K_t,d_t)->K_{t+1}; (5) Orient rho_t(K_t,Omega). The fifth (Orient) is said to become much more visible once Chapter 11 (the horizon Omega) is added to the model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \Omega = \{ Observe,\; Discriminate,\; Relate,\; Validate,\; Qualify,\; Transform,\; Reject,\; Accept,\; Revise \}
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate (non-canonical) operator family from Chapters 10-15 combined: Omega={Observe, Discriminate, Relate, Validate, Qualify, Transform, Reject, Accept, Revise}, with Buddhi approx delta as the mechanism selecting/executing several of these, e.g. delta(Observation,Context)->Decision and delta(K_t,E_t)->K_{t+1}, connecting to the unresolved Qualify problem from Steps 285-287.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal K \neq K_t \neq \mathcal M
b_rows_sample.statement: Formal first principle: K (Knowledge Space, potentially unbounded) != K_t (Knowledge State at time t, what the system currently represents) != M (KnowledgeOS Kernel, the smallest persistent computational unit that evaluates and transforms knowledge states). The Gita's language helps interpret M as Mind, but the software kernel is not literally the philosophical mind. Defines M = the smallest unit capable of epistemic state transition, i.e. capable of K_t->K_{t+1} under some evidence/observation/proposition/event/operation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Z:\boxed{K_t\rightarrow G_t} ... \delta: \boxed{(K_t,G_t,E_t,C_t)\rightarrow D_t} ... \tau: \boxed{(K_t,D_t)\rightarrow K_{t+1}}
b_rows_sample.statement: Full typed operator pipeline: Z:K_t->G_t (gap/boundary discovery, internal inspection); delta:(K_t,G_t,E_t,C_t)->D_t (discrimination/Buddhi, taking gaps, evidence, and context); tau:(K_t,D_t)->K_{t+1} (transition/transformation). Composition tau o delta o Z is type-correct given matching interfaces; for external input f_x(K_t)=tau(K_t,delta(x,E,C)); for internally discovered gaps f_Z(K_t)=tau(K_t,delta(Z(K_t))). The kernel therefore performs two fundamentally different activities: external epistemic input (x->delta) and internal epistemic inspection (K_t--Z-->G_t).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Level 0 — Primitive kernel mechanisms ... Level 1 — epistemic operations ... Level 2 — higher-order processes
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a three-level operator hierarchy to address the concern that not all candidate operators should be primitive: Level 0 primitives {delta,Z,tau} (smallest candidates); Level 1 epistemic operations built from primitives (Observe, Compare, Validate, Qualify, Revise, Accept, Reject), e.g. Accept(x)=tau(K_t,delta(x,E,C)=accepted), Reject(x)=tau(K_t,delta(x,E,C)=rejected); Level 2 higher-order processes as compositions (Purification, Learning, Investigation, Knowledge evolution), P = O_1 o O_2 o ... o O_n, assessed as important for DDD (avoiding conflating primitive operations with their compositions).

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathcal M=(Q,\mathbb O,\delta,\tau,\mathbb I)
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes formalizing the kernel as a state machine M=(Q,O,delta,tau,I) where Q=kernel control states (renamed from S to avoid collision with Sigma's S axis), O=kernel operations, delta=discrimination function, tau=transition function, I=invariants. Also proposes the kernel invariant M != K_t must hold (otherwise K_t->K_{t+1} would mean the kernel becomes a different object every time); formalized as Identity(M_t)=Identity(M_{t+1}) while K_t != K_{t+1} is permitted -- 'persistent kernel identity + mutable epistemic state' proposed as a fundamental candidate architectural invariant, worth testing against the corpus.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Qualify: X\rightarrow \{Qualified,\;Unqualified,\;Terminated\} ... Kernel determines the admissible epistemic status of a state transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines Qualify (still classified G1) via the Cavell insight (justification may legitimately terminate rather than being infinitely extended) into Qualify:X->{Qualified, Unqualified, Terminated}, rather than assuming qualification is always a total true/false decision -- candidate only. Reframes the kernel's deeper job away from 'determine truth' toward 'Kernel determines the admissible epistemic status of a state transition', assessed as much closer to what the corpus actually supports; enumerates the kernel's operative questions (what do we have, what evidence supports it, what is missing, what conflicts, what relationship exists, what can legitimately be concluded, where must qualification stop, what state transition is admissible).

a_notations: Y_purify = Q o C o R o E o Z

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'epistemic-purification-operator-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'step291-kernel-operation-algebra-proposal' (batch B0054). Note: Reframes purification/Moksha not as adding knowledge but as a multidimensional transformation: dimension expansion (D_t subset D_{t+1}) plus dimension refinement (v_t(d) preceq_d v_{t+1}(d)) under per-dimension order relations. Proposes six candidate operators E(xpansion), R(efinement), C(orrection), X (contradiction resolution), Q(ualify), Z(ero detection), studies their non-commutative composition algebra (closure/associativity/non-commutativity, e.g. E o Q != Q o E), reframes Yoga as operator composition trajectories (Y_purify = Q o C o R o E o Z), argues purification is a partially-ordered trajectory not a scalar purity score, and reformulates Moksha as Moksha = lim_{t->T} Purify(K_t) rather than max(K), posing a 5-question Epistemic Purification Algebra research programme.

explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'epistemic-purification-operator-algebra' POSSIBLY relates to 'step291-kernel-operation-algebra-proposal' (batch B0055). Note: The purification-as-multidimensional-quality-transformation hypothesis, first proposed in B0054; reused and substantially extended throughout B0055's kernel-model track (dimension/value/topology/probability formulations).
