a_rows_sample.anchor: Y=natively representable, P=representable only with an added construction, N=not representable. ... | assertions | Y | Y | P | Y | N | Y |
a_rows_sample.statement: Executed 17-capability x 6-model capability matrix (Y/P/N scale) testing Step 231's six candidate K models (A Set, B Graph, C Probabilistic, D Typed-proposition, E Lattice, F Hybrid) against assertions/evidence/provenance/context/contradiction/uncertainty/temporal-evolution/supersession/authority/validation/unknown/missingness/non-identifiability/governance/lineage/replay/state-transition, yielding scores (Y+0.5P): A=4.0, B=10.0, C=6.0, D=12.0, E=5.0, F=14.5.

a_rows_sample.anchor: authority A:N B:P C:N D:P E:N ... K should NOT carry authority, validation, governance or replay. Every attempt to make a single structure represent them forces a P.
a_rows_sample.statement: Principal result: four capabilities (authority, validation, governance, replay) are natively representable (Y) by NO model at all, including the hybrid Model F which scores only P on all four -- interpreted not as a model deficiency but as evidence these four are not properties of a knowledge state at all: Authority is a relation between actor and action (a property of a transformation, not a state), Validation is an external assessment of a state (a state cannot validate itself without circularity), Governance is a relation between policy and transformation, and Replay is a property of a history of transformations, not any single state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: This vindicates the kernel's shape while refuting Model F. \mathcal K=(K,C,T,E,A) is right to keep A separate from K -- and Model F is wrong to try to absorb everything into K.
a_rows_sample.statement: The four-capability result vindicates Step 230's kernel decision to keep Authority A separate from K while directly refuting Step 231's own preferred hybrid Model F for trying to absorb authority (among other things) into K -- Steps 230 and 231's proposals are shown to be in unnoticed tension, and the matrix independently confirms the mandate's own hint that the correct answer may be a typed family of related structures rather than one tuple.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K = {(q,s,e,c,t,u)} ... with authority, validation, governance and replay held OUTSIDE K -- in A, in assessment operations, in Policy, and in History(T) respectively. Status: VERIFIER RECOMMENDS / PROPOSED RECONSTRUCTION.
a_rows_sample.statement: Model D (typed proposition tuples K={(q,s,e,c,t)}) is the executed-matrix-strongest single structure (8 Y's, only 1 N: non-identifiability); the derived (not corpus-established) recommendation augments it with an uncertainty annotation u to cover that gap: K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)}, with authority/validation/governance/replay explicitly held outside K -- a refinement of, not an invention beyond, the corpus's own Model D candidate, explicitly flagged VERIFIER RECOMMENDS, not CORPUS ESTABLISHES.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A REFUTED as adequate ... B PARTIALLY ADEQUATE ... C REFUTED as a general model; NECESSARY as a component ... D STRONGEST SINGLE MODEL ... E REFUTED as adequate ... F UNDER-SPECIFIED.
a_rows_sample.statement: Model-by-model verdicts: A (bare set) refuted as adequate, carrying no provenance/context/uncertainty/evidence; B (graph) partially adequate, strong on relational concerns but cannot express uncertainty or non-identifiability; C (probabilistic) refuted as a general model yet necessary as a component (only model natively handling uncertainty AND non-identifiability); D (typed propositions) strongest single model; E (lattice/order) refuted as adequate, a relation ON knowledge states not a model OF one; F (hybrid) under-specified -- scores highest only because it is a list of six structures with no integration rule, no stated typing, no interaction semantics, no equality, no membership.

a_rows_sample.anchor: it re-introduces the E double-binding recorded in KERNEL-AUDIT-230-232.md §7 -- Evidence appears inside K here while also being kernel component E.
a_rows_sample.statement: Model F (the corpus's own preferred candidate) is cross-referenced as re-introducing the Evidence double-binding defect already recorded in the separate KERNEL-AUDIT-230-232 report: Evidence appears both inside K (via Model F) and as the separate sibling kernel component E, with no stated distinction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K is currently undefined | CORPUS ESTABLISHES ... Model F is the answer | SOURCE CLAIM -- asserted, not argued ... Model D is the strongest single structure | VERIFIED (executed matrix)
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit corpus-vs-audit evidence-class table separating what the corpus itself establishes (K is undefined; six candidate models are worth testing) from what is merely a source claim (Model F is the answer, asserted not argued) versus what this audit independently VERIFIES (no model natively carries authority/validation/governance/replay; those four belong outside K; Model D is the strongest single structure) versus what the audit only RECOMMENDS (the augmented K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)} form).

a_rows_sample.anchor: No integration rule for Model F. Until one exists, F is not a mathematical object. ... K_1=K_2 is never given a criterion, which blocks Replay, Merge and Supersede in Step 232's algebra.
a_rows_sample.statement: Open issues: Model F has no integration rule and so is not yet a mathematical object; equality and identity on K are undefined in ALL six models (K1=K2 has no criterion anywhere), which blocks Step 232's Replay/Merge/Supersede algebra operations; Model D's status field s has no declared value set, and the corpus carries eleven competing epistemic-status vocabularies (tracked as TV-F-074), so Model D cannot be instantiated until one is chosen.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Model A -- Set model K\subseteq X. ... Model F -- Hybrid model K=(Graph, Types, Propositions, Evidence, Probability, Time). We should not select the most mathematically sophisticated model merely because it is sophisticated.
b_rows_sample.statement: Step 231 (tail) poses 'what is K?' and lists six competing candidate representations of a knowledge state: A) Set model K subseteq X, B) Graph model K=(V,E), C) Probabilistic model K~P_theta, D) Typed proposition model K={(q,s,e,c,t)}, E) Lattice/ordered model K1<=K2, F) Hybrid model K=(Graph,Types,Propositions,Evidence,Probability,Time); explicitly warns against selecting the most sophisticated model merely for its sophistication, and poses the key question of the smallest structure able to represent knowledge/uncertainty/context/provenance/contradiction/change/verification without collapsing their distinct meanings.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K=everything the system knows. This is unusable. ... would contradict the epistemic distinctions we established in Steps 228-230.
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicit rejection of the naive starting definition K='everything the system knows', which mixes observations, documents, claims, hypotheses, decisions, rules, code, architecture, evidence, interpretations and AI output into an undifferentiated repository, contradicting the epistemic distinctions established in Steps 228-230.

b_rows_sample.anchor: k=(q,s,c,t,\sigma,\lambda) where q=proposition, s=epistemic status, c=context, t=temporal validity, \sigma=support/evidence, \lambda=lineage.
b_rows_sample.statement: A knowledge assertion is formalized as the 6-tuple k=(q,s,c,t,sigma,lambda): proposition/content, epistemic status, context, temporal validity, support/evidence, lineage -- substantially better than k=q alone.

b_rows_sample.anchor: S=\{Observed,Reported,Inferred,Proposed,Validated,Accepted,Superseded,Rejected\}. Content\neq EpistemicStatus.
b_rows_sample.statement: Epistemic status s in a provisional 8-value set S={Observed,Reported,Inferred,Proposed,Validated,Accepted,Superseded,Rejected}, with the architectural property Content != EpistemicStatus -- the same proposition can move through several states, e.g. Proposed->Validated->Accepted->Superseded.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \delta:S\times Event\rightarrow S. ... \delta(Proposed,ValidationPassed)=Validated.
b_rows_sample.statement: Epistemic status forms a state-transition system: delta:S x Event -> S, e.g. delta(Proposed,ValidationPassed)=Validated -- already implementable and testable, and DDD-interpretable as a KnowledgeItem domain object whose lifecycle (Identity, Proposition, Context, EpistemicStatus, Validity, EvidenceReferences, Lineage) matters, with the invariant 'a material epistemic state transition must be represented'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K\subseteq X. ... Set model alone is insufficient. ... G_K=(V,E). ... Graph model is necessary in many cases, but not sufficient. ... K\sim P_\theta. ... Knowledge\neq ProbabilityDistribution.
b_rows_sample.statement: Systematic elimination of single-structure candidate models for K: Set model (K subseteq X) captures membership but loses ordering/provenance/contradiction/uncertainty/history; Graph model (G_K=(V,E)) captures relationships naturally but not uncertainty/epistemic-status/temporal validity/probability; Probabilistic model (K~P_theta) is useful for uncertain phenomena but most architecture statements (e.g. 'Class X extends Y') are deterministic structural facts, not distributions -- Knowledge != ProbabilityDistribution; probability is a property of some knowledge, not its universal representation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K=(V,E,\tau,\pi) where V=typed knowledge nodes, E=typed relationships, \tau=type function, \pi=epistemic/provenance metadata.
b_rows_sample.statement: Typed proposition model combined with a graph gives K=(V,E,tau,pi): typed knowledge nodes, typed relationships (e.g. tau(v)=Requirement, edge=(v1,supports,v2)), a type function, and epistemic/provenance metadata; worked example Requirement -motivates-> ArchitectureDecision <-supports- TestEvidence illustrates it is far more expressive than a document repository.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A_1\xleftrightarrow{contradicts}A_2. Then governance can determine what happens. ... Contradiction\neq SystemFailure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Contradiction must be representable as a first-class relation (A1 <-contradicts-> A2) before classical truth resolution is forced, and governance then determines the outcome; Contradiction != SystemFailure -- conflicting claims may differ by context, time, superseding, assumptions, error, or genuine domain uncertainty, making contradiction often an epistemic state requiring resolution rather than a bug.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \llbracket q_A\rrbracket_{C_A} and \llbracket q_B\rrbracket_{C_B}. This is precisely where bounded contexts become mathematically significant.
b_rows_sample.statement: Context resolves many apparent contradictions: q_A valid in C_A and q_B valid in C_B with q_A != q_B does not necessarily imply inconsistency once evaluated via their context-relative denotations [[q_A]]_CA and [[q_B]]_CB -- the point at which bounded contexts become mathematically significant.

b_rows_sample.anchor: False\neq Superseded. ... Validity(k)=[t_{start},t_{end}). Current(k,t)\iff t\in Validity(k).
b_rows_sample.statement: Temporal knowledge: False != Superseded (a superseded proposition q_2025 is not necessarily false, merely no longer current), formalized via Validity(k)=[t_start,t_end) and Current(k,t) iff t in Validity(k) -- giving temporal semantics to knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1}=T(K_t,C,E,A,P). ... T_t:(K_t,C_t,E_t,A_t,P_t)\rightarrow K_{t+1}.
b_rows_sample.statement: The knowledge state is dynamic: rather than a static K, K_t evolves via a governed transformation T_t:(K_t,C_t,E_t,A_t,P_t)->K_{t+1}, becoming the central state-transition equation connecting directly to the transformation-centric architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t=(G_t,\Sigma_t,\Theta_t,\Lambda_t). ... K_t=(G_t,\Sigma_t,\Theta_t,\Lambda_t,\Pi_t). ... KnowledgeOS should not force knowledge into one mathematical datatype.
b_rows_sample.statement: The knowledge state is defined as a hybrid mathematical structure, first as a 4-tuple K_t=(G_t semantic graph, Sigma_t epistemic assignments, Theta_t temporal validity structure, Lambda_t provenance/lineage) then extended to 5 layers with Pi_t (probabilistic/uncertainty information): no single conventional mathematical object (graph, logic, time, probability, provenance) alone captures all required dimensions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: G_t=(V_t,E_t) ... \tau_V, \tau_E ... motivates, supports, contradicts, refines, implements, supersedes.
b_rows_sample.statement: Layer 1 (Semantic graph): G_t=(V_t,E_t) with node-type function tau_V and relation-type function tau_E over named relation types {motivates, supports, contradicts, refines, implements, supersedes}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \sigma:V_t\rightarrow S. ... This prevents content and status from being conflated.
b_rows_sample.statement: Layer 2 (Epistemic state): sigma:V_t -> S assigns each node an epistemic status (e.g. Accepted, Proposed), preventing content and status conflation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \theta:V_t\rightarrow TimeIntervals. ... historically valid from currently valid.
b_rows_sample.statement: Layer 3 (Temporal validity): theta:V_t -> TimeIntervals (e.g. theta(v)=[2026-01-01,2026-07-01)) distinguishes historically valid from currently valid.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \lambda(v) as a provenance subgraph. Requirement\leftarrow Meeting\leftarrow Observation\leftarrow Source.
b_rows_sample.statement: Layer 4 (Provenance): lambda(v) is a provenance subgraph (e.g. Requirement<-Meeting<-Observation<-Source) reconstructing why a knowledge item exists.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \pi(v) can represent uncertainty. ... The architecture must not force all uncertainty into a number.
b_rows_sample.statement: Layer 5 (Uncertainty): pi(v) may represent a probability, confidence interval, likelihood, or qualitative uncertainty category -- explicitly must not force all uncertainty into a single number.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Number\neq Probability. Confidence\neq Truth. KnowledgeOS should carry the semantics of the uncertainty measure.
b_rows_sample.statement: Important statistical principle: a confidence score like 0.83 is meaningless without defining what it means (model probability? expert confidence? empirical accuracy? posterior? heuristic ranking?) -- Number != Probability and Confidence != Truth; the uncertainty measure's semantics must be carried explicitly.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \mathfrak K_t=(G_t,\sigma_t,\theta_t,\lambda_t,\pi_t) as the candidate mathematical representation of a knowledge state. ... It is a candidate Knowledge State Algebra.
b_rows_sample.statement: The candidate mathematical knowledge-state object is finalized as mathfrak K_t=(G_t,sigma_t,theta_t,lambda_t,pi_t), explicitly named a candidate Knowledge State Algebra (not yet a final theorem), with transformation T_t: mathfrak K_t x C_t x E_t x A_t x P_t -> mathfrak K_{t+1} as the most complete formulation so far.

b_rows_sample.anchor: \Delta_t=(\Delta_t^+,\Delta_t^-,\Delta_t^\sim).
b_rows_sample.statement: Transformation delta is decomposed rather than treated as naive graph subtraction: Delta_t = (Delta_t^+ additions, Delta_t^- removals, Delta_t^~ modifications) -- a much better representation of change.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from system boundary to the inside of the system. Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence. A component is therefore not defined merely by its directory or class name.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence, stating a component is not defined merely by its directory or class name.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.1 — Component reconstruction principle ... C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner). Only after these are established can we decide whether two components are separate, overlapping, duplicates, parts of one bounded context
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the full component reconstruction tuple C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner), a precondition for classifying inter-component relationships.

type_signature.codomain: Identity x Purpose x Responsibilities x Data x Commands x Queries x Dependencies x Interfaces x Invariants x Tests x Runtime x Owner

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.2 — First question: what is a component? ... Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext. They are not equivalent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes seven frequently-confused units of analysis: Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.3 — Experiment 1 ... Repository contains KnowledgeService.java. Can we conclude KnowledgeService=KnowledgeBoundedContext? No. It may simply be an application service. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a KnowledgeService.java class does not by itself establish a KnowledgeBoundedContext; it may be merely an application service; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.4 — Component levels ... System→BoundedContext→{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, plus Supporting Systems. This prevents accidental conflation of implementation structure and domain structure.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a multi-level reconstruction tree (System->BoundedContext->{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, Supporting Systems) preventing conflation of implementation and domain structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.5 — Component identity ... ComponentID should not depend solely on ClassName. Because names change.
a_rows_sample.statement: States component identity must be stable and independent of class naming, since names change.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.6 — Experiment 2 ... Class KnowledgeService becomes EngineeringKnowledgeService. Expected: potentially the same logical component. Result: PASS. This is why logical identity and implementation naming must be separated.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: a renamed class (KnowledgeService to EngineeringKnowledgeService) may remain the same logical component; result PASS, motivating separation of logical identity from naming.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.7 — Responsibility reconstruction ... What responsibility does this component actually own? Not what does its README claim? We inspect Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies.
a_rows_sample.statement: States responsibility must be reconstructed from actual Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies, not from README claims.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.8 — Experiment 3 ... Component named KnowledgeManager actually reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data. Expected: observed responsibility closer to KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing than KnowledgeAuthority. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a KnowledgeManager's actual behavior (reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data) reveals its real responsibility as KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing rather than KnowledgeAuthority; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.9 — Responsibility is more important than naming ... ObservedBehavior > ComponentName for determining actual responsibility.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the central rule ObservedBehavior>ComponentName for determining actual component responsibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.10 — Data ownership ... Which data does the component own? We distinguish Reads(Data) from Owns(Data). A service can read data without owning it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Reads(Data) from Owns(Data): a service reading data does not thereby own it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.11 — Experiment 4 ... Component A reads Decision. Component B creates and changes Decision. Expected: B is the stronger candidate for ownership. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: the component that creates and changes Decision (B) is the stronger ownership candidate over one that merely reads it (A); result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.12 — Data ownership graph ... Component-owns->Data and separately Component-reads->Data. This becomes crucial for determining bounded-context boundaries.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the data-ownership graph with separate owns and reads edge types, crucial for bounded-context boundary determination.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.13 — Experiment 5 ... Two services directly modify the same decision table. Expected: potential shared-data coupling. Result: OBS. This does not yet prove architectural failure, but it is an important finding.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: two services directly mutating the same decision table is potential shared-data coupling, classified OBS (an important finding, not yet a proven failure).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.14 — Aggregate ownership ... Aggregate→Invariant→Owner. Decision may own invariants such as Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the aggregate-ownership model Aggregate→Invariant→Owner, illustrated by Decision owning Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.15 — Experiment 6 ... Two unrelated services can independently set decision.status=APPROVED without passing through a common invariant boundary. Expected: potential aggregate-boundary violation. Result: OBS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: two independent services both able to set decision.status=APPROVED without a shared invariant boundary is a potential aggregate-boundary violation, classified OBS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.16 — Command ownership ... Command→OwningComponent. CreateEvidence, ApproveDecision, RegisterAgent, RecordObservation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines command ownership Command→OwningComponent, with example commands CreateEvidence/ApproveDecision/RegisterAgent/RecordObservation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.17 — Experiment 7 ... Both Service A and Service B implement ApproveDecision. Expected: potential duplicate business responsibility. Result: OBS. This is exactly the kind of issue the actual inventory should expose.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: two services both implementing ApproveDecision is potential duplicate business responsibility, classified OBS, exemplifying the inventory's diagnostic purpose.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.18 — Query ownership ... Query→OwningSource. But multiple read models may legitimately expose the same information. DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership.
a_rows_sample.statement: States DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership: multiple read models exposing the same information may be legitimate rather than duplicated ownership.

a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a UI-projection GET /decisions endpoint alongside an authoritative domain API endpoint is not automatically duplicate domain capability; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from component architecture to semantic architecture. What meaning does each component actually own? The central chain is Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→BoundedContext.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the central semantic-ownership chain Data→Meaning→Invariant→Owner→BoundedContext, shifting from component to semantic architecture.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.1 — Data is not knowledge ... Data≠Knowledge. A row in a database is data. Knowledge requires semantic interpretation. 'ADR-042 was approved on 2026-08-12.' can represent Decision with subject, authority, timestamp, rationale, status, provenance.
b_rows_sample.statement: States Data≠Knowledge: raw data (rows, documents, embeddings, logs) requires semantic interpretation to become knowledge, illustrated by an ADR-approval string requiring subject/authority/timestamp/rationale/status/provenance to constitute a Decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.2 — Experiment 1 ... Database contains status=APPROVED. Can we conclude that an authorized decision exists? Not necessarily. We need WhoApproved, UnderWhichAuthority, When, WhatWasApproved, WhatEvidenceSupportsIt. Result: PASS. A field value is not sufficient semantic evidence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a bare status=APPROVED field value does not establish an authorized decision without who/under-what-authority/when/what/evidence; result PASS, a field value is not sufficient semantic evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.3 — Semantic object ... Concept=(Identity,Meaning,State,Invariants,Relationships,Authority,Provenance). This becomes the basis for identifying genuine domain objects.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the semantic object tuple Concept=(Identity,Meaning,State,Invariants,Relationships,Authority,Provenance) as the basis for identifying genuine domain objects.

type_signature.codomain: Identity x Meaning x State x Invariants x Relationships x Authority x Provenance

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.4 — Candidate concepts ... evidence, observations, claims, decisions, rules, architecture, agents, changes, findings, verification. But ConceptMention≠ConceptImplementation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Lists ten candidate semantic concepts and states ConceptMention≠ConceptImplementation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.5 — Experiment 2 ... The word Evidence appears in EvidenceCollector, EvidenceStore, EvidenceReport, EvidenceAPI. Expected: this establishes terminology, not yet a coherent Evidence domain. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: four classes naming 'Evidence' establish terminology only, not proof of a coherent Evidence domain; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.6 — Semantic definition ... What does this thing mean? Evidence=information that supports or constrains a claim. But the actual implementation may define it differently. The repository's actual semantics must therefore be reconstructed.
b_rows_sample.statement: States each candidate concept's meaning must be reconstructed from actual implementation semantics rather than an assumed definition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.7 — Experiment 3 ... Module A treats an 'evidence' object as a source document. Module B treats 'evidence' as a runtime observation. Expected: potential semantic collision. Result: OBS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: Module A treating evidence as a source document versus Module B treating it as a runtime observation is a potential semantic collision, classified OBS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.8 — Meaning boundary ... If two contexts use the same word differently: Evidence_A≠Evidence_B. That may be perfectly legitimate if the contexts are distinct. The problem arises when the system treats them as the same concept without an explicit translation.
b_rows_sample.statement: States Evidence_A≠Evidence_B across distinct contexts may be legitimate; the problem arises only when treated as the same concept without explicit translation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.9 — Bounded Context hypothesis ... A bounded context exists when a coherent semantic model owns Concepts+Rules+Invariants+Language. Therefore BoundedContext≠Directory.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a bounded context as existing where a coherent semantic model owns Concepts+Rules+Invariants+Language, stating BoundedContext≠Directory.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.10 — Experiment 4 ... A directory is named evidence/ but contains only file parsing, OCR, embeddings. Expected: this may be an ingestion/indexing component, not necessarily an Evidence bounded context. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: an 'evidence/' directory containing only file parsing/OCR/embeddings may be ingestion infrastructure, not an Evidence bounded context; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.11 — Semantic ownership ... Who owns the meaning? Not merely who stores the record? EvidenceRepository may store evidence. But EvidenceDomain should define what evidence means and what makes it valid.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes semantic ownership as 'who owns the meaning' distinct from 'who stores the record,' illustrated by EvidenceRepository (storage) vs EvidenceDomain (meaning/validity definition).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.12 — Experiment 5 ... Three services write evidence records. Only one defines evidence validation rules. Expected: the validating service is the stronger semantic owner candidate. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: among three evidence-writing services, the one defining validation rules is the stronger semantic-owner candidate; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.13 — Invariants identify ownership ... Invariant→Owner. Claim⇒EvidenceRequired. The component enforcing that rule is a strong candidate for owning the relevant semantic boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: States Invariant->Owner as one of the strongest ownership-identification techniques, illustrated by Claim⇒EvidenceRequired.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.14 — Experiment 6 ... Two components manipulate a Decision. Only one enforces Approved⇒AuthorityPresent. Expected: that component likely owns the decision invariant. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: among two Decision-manipulating components, the one enforcing Approved⇒AuthorityPresent likely owns the decision invariant; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.15 — State transitions ... Candidate→Reviewed→Verified→Authoritative. Who is allowed to perform each transition? That reveals the governance boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: States that authorized state-transition performers (Candidate->Reviewed->Verified->Authoritative) reveal the governance boundary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.16 — Experiment 7 ... Any component can transition Candidate→Authoritative. Expected: potential semantic/governance defect. Result: OBS/VIOLATION depending on the actual intended rule.
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: any component being able to directly transition Candidate to Authoritative is a potential semantic/governance defect, classified OBS/VIOLATION depending on intended rule.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.17 — Identity ... DecisionID must remain stable even if wording changes, representation changes, document location changes.
b_rows_sample.statement: States decision identity (DecisionID) must remain stable across wording/representation/location changes.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.18 — Experiment 8 ... Decision is identified only by filename ADR-042.md. File is renamed. Expected: if the system treats the filename as identity, semantic identity is fragile. Result: OBS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: filename-based decision identity is fragile if the filename can be renamed; classified OBS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 112.19 — Provenance ... KnowledgeObject→Provenance. Possible provenance: document, repository, commit, runtime event, human, agent, external system.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines KnowledgeObject->Provenance with seven possible provenance types (document/repository/commit/runtime event/human/agent/external system).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Article I.1 ... Article I.2 ... Article I.3 -- Mathematics describes, never defines.
b_rows_sample.statement: Chapter I, the Constitutional Identity: Article I.1 the character (KnowledgeOS governs how knowledge is created/justified/transformed/challenged/evolved while preserving identity/context/evidence/authority/reasoning/uncertainty/agency/historical evolution); Article I.2 the three clause refinements (existence, reasoning, identity) are constitutionally absorbed as phrasing refinements, not supersessions; Article I.3 the governing maxim 'Mathematics describes, never defines' -- topology, type theory, graphs, TMS, AGM, LLMs are mechanisms/explanatory lenses, never kernel law by virtue of being mathematical or computational.

b_rows_sample.anchor: CONSTITUTIONAL KERNEL <- the eleven articles (PRESERVE) ... Engine Layer (GOVERN) ... Mechanisms (GOVERN) ... Representations (ENABLE) ... Implementation (ENABLE)
b_rows_sample.statement: Chapter III, the Kernel Boundary: a 5-tier diagram -- Constitutional Kernel (the 11 articles, PRESERVE) served by Engine Layer (validation engines, fallacy detection, debate pipeline, intent classification, verdict vocabulary, GOVERN), Mechanisms (epistemic-inquiry lifecycle, reasoning pipelines, GOVERN), Representations (evidence records, context tuples, epistemic state model, absence taxonomy, epistemic graph, typed encodings, ENABLE), and Implementation (storage, interfaces, systems, deliberately unconstrained, ENABLE). III.1 the kernel does not do the reasoning -- it states what must be preserved/never collapse; engines execute governed transformations realizing those constraints. III.2 no engine/mechanism/representation may violate an article -- evolution that violates an article is a corruption, not an evolution, subject to Chapter V. III.3 implementation is deliberately out of constitutional scope.

b_rows_sample.anchor: V.1 Engineering evolution -- no amendment required. ... V.2 Constitutional amendment -- required ... V.3 What amendment MAY do ... V.4 Ratification.
b_rows_sample.statement: Chapter V, Amendment Discipline (new content, not present verbatim in any prior artifact in this file group): engines/mechanisms/representations/implementation (Chapter III) MAY evolve freely provided no evolution violates an article (V.1); the 11 articles, the character, the negative boundary, and the kernel/engine boundary SHALL NOT change except by HPA-ratified constitutional amendment, and no article SHALL be weakened (V.2); amendment MAY refine wording, correct inconsistency, or -- on evidence a specific corruption is unguarded -- add a strengthening clause, but SHALL NOT add new concepts/sources/rows ('the corpus that produced this Constitution is closed; adding knowledge to the kernel would violate the discipline this Constitution establishes', V.3); amendment is effective only by HPA ruling following the same evidence/domain-independence/necessity/failure-test discipline that produced step 5 (V.4).

a_rows_sample.anchor: What are we actually building when we say "KnowledgeOS"? ... None of these individually is "knowledge." ... our work has actually been a process of negative-space discovery ... what KnowledgeOS must not confuse with knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Surveys ~27 concepts explored across the whole lens series (words, sentences, topics, documents, embeddings, propositions, facts, observations, evidence, assertions, questions, answers, truth, uncertainty, coherence, relevance, completeness, boundaries, time, inference, semantics, Pramana, Dhatu, Karaka, Paninian grammar, statistical inference, ML, topology, critical thinking, consciousness analogy, DDD bounded contexts), concluding none individually is 'knowledge'; reframes the whole research program as 'negative-space discovery' -- discovering what KnowledgeOS must not confuse with knowledge -- noting the DDD review (S0508) reaches the same conclusion (the model was crossing semantic/linguistic/evidence/inquiry/assessment/governance concerns, not describing one domain).

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would now reject this model: KnowledgeOS |-- Topics -- Words -- Sentences -- Documents -- Facts -- Truth. ... KnowledgeOS is a system for maintaining the semantic, epistemic and contextual integrity of a changing body of knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects three candidate definitions of KnowledgeOS (a knowledge database of topics/words/sentences/documents/facts/truth -- 'basically a sophisticated content management system'; a KnowledgeGraph, since a graph is a representation structure not necessarily knowledge; AI memory, since memory is only one retention mechanism), replacing them with 'KnowledgeOS is a system for maintaining the semantic, epistemic and contextual integrity of a changing body of knowledge', illustrated by an eighteen-question list (what does this mean? who claims it? what evidence supports it? can we reconstruct why we currently believe this? etc).

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel should NOT contain "all knowledge" ... The Kernel should not own the world model. It should own the rules and structures that make a knowledge system trustworthy. ... The kernel is therefore closer to an epistemic infrastructure than a knowledge repository.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the file's most important architectural conclusion: the Kernel must not own the world model, only the rules/structures making a knowledge system trustworthy (identity, semantics, provenance, boundaries, temporal validity, assertions, evidence relations, epistemic status, inquiry structures, assessment records, invariants), positioned between the external world (via observations/sources) and downstream consumers (AI Agent, Developer, Human) via projections -- the Kernel is an epistemic infrastructure, not a knowledge repository.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A. Identity ... string ≠ semantic object; embedding ≠ identity; sentence ≠ proposition. ... B. Meaning/semantic structure ... The kernel should not contain every domain concept. ... C. Epistemic integrity ... Observation ≠ Fact ≠ Proposition ≠ Assertion ≠ Truth. ... D. Inquiry ... E. Assessment ... Assessment is an act performed under a regime.
a_rows_sample.statement: Divides the Kernel into five fundamental capabilities: (A) Identity -- stable semantic identity (SemanticIdentity/ConceptIdentity/PropositionIdentity/AssertionIdentity/BoundaryIdentity), since string!=semantic object, embedding!=identity, sentence!=proposition; (B) Meaning/semantic structure -- Concept/Relation/Proposition/Constraint/Type as semantic machinery, explicitly not every domain's vocabulary (banking's Account/Transaction/Customer vs election's Voter/Ballot/Result remain domain knowledge, matching the DDD review's semantic-modeling-context recommendation); (C) Epistemic integrity -- Assertion/Evidence/Observation/Inference/Provenance/TemporalValidity/EpistemicStatus/Conflict, with Observation!=Fact!=Proposition!=Assertion!=Truth as an essential separation (matching the DDD review's state-of-affairs/observation-record/assertion/evidence distinction); (D) Inquiry -- Question/QuestionOperator/Target/Scope/Constraints/Presuppositions/AnswerObligations as structural (not domain-specific) kernel capability; (E) Assessment -- infrastructure for recording semantic-admissibility/truth-status/epistemic-status/coherence/relevance/answerability/completeness/uncertainty/conflict as an act performed under a regime (Assessment{proposition,regime,context,evidence,evaluatedAt,result}), not a mutable Proposition.truth=TRUE field.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Natural language generation ... The Dhātu/Pāṇinian work belongs here. ... Embeddings ... embedding ≠ semantic identity. ... Statistical/ML models ... the statistical model itself should not become kernel ontology. ... Domain knowledge ... The kernel should support them. It should not own them. ... Documents ... Mostly outside.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly places six categories outside the Kernel: natural language generation/LLMs/translation/summarization/Sanskrit-Paninian parsing (an interpretation/compiler layer); embeddings (useful for similarity/retrieval/clustering/search/classification, but embedding != semantic identity); statistical/ML models (Bayesian/regression/classification/clustering/PCA/manifold-learning/graph-ML/neural-networks/LLMs -- kernel records their results/provenance, not the models themselves); domain knowledge (election/banking/insurance/hotel/engineering/medicine/law -- kernel supports, does not own); user interfaces; and documents (mostly outside -- kernel knows a representation exists and how it relates to semantic/epistemic objects, without becoming a document management system).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Boundary 1 — Semantic boundary ... Boundary 2 — Context boundary ... "Result" ... Election context / Analytics context / Legal context ... Boundary 3 — Epistemic boundary ... what exists in the world vs what our knowledge system currently has grounds to claim. ... Boundary 4 — System boundary ... KnowledgeOS guarantees the integrity of knowledge representations and their epistemic relationships. It does NOT guarantee that the external world itself is true.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes four previously-conflated senses of 'boundary': Semantic boundary (which concepts belong to a domain model, e.g. Election's Voter/Ballot/Candidate/Result); Context boundary (which interpretation of a concept is active -- 'Result' meaning official outcome in Election context, statistical result in Analytics context, legally certified outcome in Legal context); Epistemic boundary (KNOWN/UNKNOWN/UNCERTAIN/DISPUTED/UNEXPLORED -- the line between what exists in the world and what the knowledge system currently has grounds to claim); System boundary (what KnowledgeOS guarantees architecturally -- it guarantees the integrity of knowledge representations and epistemic relationships, but never that the external world itself is true, so it can say 'under regime R, using evidence E, at time T, within context C, this assertion has status X' but never 'this statement is objectively true' -- called epistemically honest).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Kernel = what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims about reality. ... a much more precise architectural proposition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Rejects 'Knowledge Kernel = where knowledge lives' in favor of 'Knowledge Kernel = what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims about reality', called a much more precise architectural proposition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A knowledge state is a temporally situated projection whose contents and relationships can change as new observations, assertions, evidence, interpretations and assessments arrive. ... What changed? Why did it change? What evidence caused the change? ... this may ultimately be one of the deepest Kernel responsibilities.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identifies CHANGE as a missing dimension not yet adequately modeled, refining 'knowledge is a piece of continuously changing facts' into 'a knowledge state is a temporally situated projection whose contents and relationships can change as new observations, assertions, evidence, interpretations and assessments arrive' (KnowledgeState(t1)->Delta->KnowledgeState(t2)->Delta->KnowledgeState(t3)), requiring the kernel to explain what changed, why, what evidence caused it, which assertion/interpretation/boundary/assessment was superseded, and who/what performed the change -- called possibly one of the deepest Kernel responsibilities.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would NOT freeze this yet ... I would not create an ADR saying "this is the KnowledgeOS Kernel." Instead, I would create a discovery artifact: KOS — Kernel Boundary Discovery ... Semantic identity: Likely yes ... Word: No ... Knowledge state: Projection/hypothesis.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly declines to freeze an ADR declaring the Kernel boundary, citing the DDD review's list of items that must remain hypotheses (Proposition as fundamental primitive, Assertion as central aggregate, KnowledgeState as first-class object, a universal truth enum, a universal numeric knowledge vector, a complete question-operator taxonomy); instead proposes a 'KOS -- Kernel Boundary Discovery' artifact answering 'what minimum set of capabilities must be invariantly provided by KnowledgeOS regardless of domain, language, AI model, statistical method, or representation technology?', with a 20-row candidate classification table (e.g. Semantic identity/Concept/Evidence relation/Observation/Question: likely kernel; Proposition/Assertion: hypothesis; Truth: no universal truth engine, regime-dependent; Word/Sentence/Document/Embedding/LLM/ML model/Domain ontology/Knowledge graph: not kernel; Knowledge state: projection/hypothesis).

a_rows_sample.anchor: What is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve so that knowledge can be expressed, questioned, challenged, evaluated, changed and reconstructed without losing its identity, context, provenance or epistemic meaning? That is the real Kernel question.
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses the file's closing question, distinguished from 'how do we model knowledge?': 'what is the smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve so that knowledge can be expressed, questioned, challenged, evaluated, changed and reconstructed without losing its identity, context, provenance or epistemic meaning?', calling it the real Kernel question and stating that adding more classes, ML algorithms, topology, or Sanskrit grammar without answering it only makes the model larger, not more correct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The smallest thing KnowledgeOS must preserve is an identity-bearing, contextualized assertion record. ... This is a minimum preservation unit, not necessarily the fundamental aggregate or the definition of knowledge. ... PRESERVATION UNIT / CONSISTENCY BOUNDARY / PROJECTION VIEW ... These must not be collapsed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues against freezing an 'AssertionAggregate' as the Kernel, distinguishing three concepts that must not be collapsed: a preservation unit (Assertion Record -- the identity-bearing, contextualized minimum unit KnowledgeOS must preserve, explicitly not necessarily the fundamental aggregate), a consistency boundary (Aggregate -- a transactional-consistency grouping), and a projection view (Knowledge State -- a derived read model); the identity-bearing-assertion-record claim is immediately qualified as a minimum preservation unit, not a definition of knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS is infrastructure for preserving, relating, evaluating and reconstructing situated semantic commitments as knowledge changes over time. ... not "store knowledge" ... not "determine truth" ... preserve -> identify -> contextualize -> relate -> evaluate -> challenge -> change -> reconstruct.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reformulates the KnowledgeOS mission as infrastructure for preserving/relating/evaluating/reconstructing situated semantic commitments as knowledge changes over time, explicitly not storing knowledge/documents, building a knowledge graph, determining truth, replacing human reasoning, or building AI memory, operationalized as an eight-step capability chain: preserve->identify->contextualize->relate->evaluate->challenge->change->reconstruct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: stable identities; immutable historical records; typed relationships; explicit context; temporal distinctions; provenance chains; epistemic and lifecycle histories; contradiction and plurality; references across bounded contexts; reconstruction capability. ... our strongest candidate for the Kernel invariant surface.
a_rows_sample.statement: Lists ten kernel principles (attributed to a referenced prior artifact) proposed as the strongest current candidate for the Kernel invariant surface: stable identities, immutable historical records, typed relationships, explicit context, temporal distinctions, provenance chains, epistemic and lifecycle histories, contradiction and plurality, cross-bounded-context references, and reconstruction capability.

a_rows_sample.anchor: what was said ... separately from what was observed ... separately from what was valid ... separately from what became effective ... separately from what was evaluated ... separately from what remains disputed. ... That generalizes beyond time. The same principle applies to the whole Kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes a referenced temporal artifact's principle (different temporal roles must not collapse into one timestamp) into a Kernel-wide principle: what-was-said, what-was-observed, what-was-valid, what-became-effective, what-was-evaluated, and what-remains-disputed must all remain separately preserved, not just temporally but across every epistemic dimension.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Assertion should not become: Assertion, truth = TRUE. Instead: Assertion: semantic identity, context, temporal claims, provenance, authority, epistemic history, lifecycle, relationships {Evidence, Question, Assessment, Contradiction, Supersession}. And an assessment says: Assessment: subject, regime, context, evidence basis, evaluator, result, uncertainty, time.
a_rows_sample.statement: Corrects a naive Assertion{truth=TRUE} model into Assertion{semantic identity, context, temporal claims, provenance, authority, epistemic history, lifecycle, relationships (Evidence/Question/Assessment/Contradiction/Supersession)} paired with a separate Assessment{subject, regime, context, evidence basis, evaluator, result, uncertainty, time}, so that evaluation is never encoded as mutating the assertion into an absolute truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS cannot guarantee: REALITY = TRUE. What it can guarantee is: "This assertion was evaluated as X under regime R, in context C, at time T, based on evidence E." That is not relativism. It is reconstructible epistemology.
a_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the project's recurring 'truth' problem via a Reality->observation->Representation->semantic interpretation->Proposition->assertion->Assertion->assessment->Epistemic Assessment chain: KnowledgeOS cannot guarantee Reality=TRUE, only that 'this assertion was evaluated as X under regime R, in context C, at time T, based on evidence E' -- explicitly distinguished from relativism and named 'reconstructible epistemology'.

a_rows_sample.anchor: "Topic" probably moves outside too ... "Kafka" can simultaneously belong to Distributed Systems, Messaging, Architecture, Infrastructure, Performance, Event Streaming, Security ... There isn't necessarily one canonical topic boundary. ... The topic is a way of looking at them.
a_rows_sample.statement: Moves Topic outside the Kernel: 'Kafka' can simultaneously belong to seven different topical groupings (Distributed Systems, Messaging, Architecture, Infrastructure, Performance, Event Streaming, Security) with no canonical topic boundary, so the Knowledge Space generates different topic projections (e.g. Architecture/Security/Operations projections) over the same underlying assertions -- Topic is a projection/context construct, not a primitive Kernel object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The KnowledgeOS Kernel boundary ends where KnowledgeOS can no longer make a domain-independent structural guarantee about the identity, context, provenance, temporal meaning, epistemic history, relationships, or reconstructibility of a knowledge-bearing assertion. ... Kernel test: If this capability is removed, can KnowledgeOS still preserve and reconstruct the identity and epistemic history of a situated semantic commitment?
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a falsifiable Kernel-boundary criterion and test: the Kernel ends where KnowledgeOS can no longer make a domain-independent structural guarantee about identity/context/provenance/temporal-meaning/epistemic-history/relationships/reconstructibility; the test for any candidate capability is 'if this capability is removed, can KnowledgeOS still preserve and reconstruct the identity and epistemic history of a situated semantic commitment?' -- yes means outside the Kernel, no means a candidate Kernel concern.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Stable identity: Yes ... Question structure: Needs boundary test ... Answer generation: Outside ... Truth determination: Outside/regime ... Topics: Probably projection ... Vector DB: Outside.
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the Kernel test to 24 candidates: yes-inside (stable identity, semantic identity/reference, context, temporal semantics [policy-driven], provenance, assertion history, epistemic history, lifecycle history, typed relationships, contradiction representation [likely]); needs-test (question structure, topics [probably projection]); outside (answer generation, truth determination, statistical inference, LLM, embedding, documents, words, sentences, domain ontology, UI, search, vector DB).

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS Kernel = the domain-independent infrastructure that preserves the identity, context, provenance, temporal semantics, epistemic history and relationships necessary to reconstruct situated semantic commitments over time. ... evaluation itself may not belong entirely inside the Kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Refines the Kernel definition from S0509's 'what makes a knowledge system capable of distinguishing, relating, evaluating and evolving claims' into 'the domain-independent infrastructure that preserves the identity, context, provenance, temporal semantics, epistemic history and relationships necessary to reconstruct situated semantic commitments over time', explicitly removing 'evaluating' from the Kernel's own responsibility since an Assertion Aggregate should not decide universal truth, objective evidence sufficiency, or universal relevance -- the Kernel provides assessment infrastructure, not the universal evaluator.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X counts as Y in context C
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes brute/natural facts from institutional facts via Searle's constitutive formula 'X counts as Y in context C', illustrated by a ballot paper counting as a vote, a person counting as a candidate, a person counting as president, and paper counting as money.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Status(X,Y,C)
b_rows_sample.statement: Refines the counts-as formula into Status(X,Y,C), described as the strongest boundary formulation reached so far, with context-sensitivity explicit: the same object can have different institutional identities in different contexts, so Status(X,Y,C1) may differ from Status(X,Y,C2), meaning context must remain explicit in the model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Searle's discussion explicitly distinguishes intrinsic properties from observer-relative and institutionally assigned functions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes intrinsic property, assigned status, and observer-relative use as three separate ways a phenomenon/object can be characterized, arguing status is not intrinsic to the object it is assigned to.

b_rows_sample.anchor: # 7. This connects directly to our "Persons and Causes" work
b_rows_sample.statement: Connects Searle's institutional layer to the earlier O'Connor Persons and Causes work by distinguishing natural/physical capacity from institutional power, and introduces 'deontic power' (rights, obligations, duties, privileges, permissions, requirements, authorizations, entitlements) as the content that institutional status can generate.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Those are not physical powers.

They are **institutional powers**.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes causal/natural power from institutional/deontic power as two fundamentally different kinds of power an agent or role-holder may have.

b_rows_sample.anchor: # 9. And this connects directly to your KnowledgeOS Constitution
b_rows_sample.statement: Connects the deontic-power concept to the project's existing Constitution/governance architecture via an Election -> Mandate -> Role -> Institutional powers -> Rights/obligations cascade.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
WORLD CHANGE
EPISTEMIC CHANGE
INSTITUTIONAL CHANGE
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a three-way knowledge-transition distinction: WORLD CHANGE, EPISTEMIC CHANGE, and INSTITUTIONAL CHANGE, as separate kinds of transition a KnowledgeOS event may represent.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Searle argues that some social/institutional facts depend on **collective intentionality** rather than simply a sum of individual beliefs.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces collective intentionality as distinct from individual intentions, arguing it feeds into institutional reality and connecting it to Fagin et al.'s common/distributed knowledge constructs.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Money -> exchange system -> property -> contract -> institutional recognition
b_rows_sample.statement: Analyzes institutional facts as relational rather than isolated: institutional facts form networks of dependency (e.g. money depends on an exchange system, which depends on property, which depends on contract, which depends on institutional recognition).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Searle explicitly argues for the **primacy of social acts/processes over social objects**.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues for the primacy of process over object in the institutional domain, directly extending the earlier Merricks 'is Assertion really an object?' question: Marriage, Government, Election, Corporation, Money, Contract, and Office are argued to be maintained practices/processes rather than inert objects.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Institutional Object
=
maintained configuration of
statuses + rules + practices + recognition
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a candidate institutional-state model for 'Corporation X' as a maintained configuration of statuses, rules, practices, and recognition, but explicitly flags this as possibly a derived projection rather than a Kernel primitive.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Searle argues that language is **constitutive** for many institutional facts, because a symbolic/representational system is required to maintain status functions
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises the project's earlier conclusion that 'language is merely an expression layer', arguing instead that language is constitutive for many institutional facts (required to maintain and communicate status functions) while not claiming all social facts require sophisticated language, yielding a refined chain: Natural/brute reality -> Social intentionality -> Status assignment -> Symbolic representation -> Institutional reality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ## Expressive language vs constitutive language
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes expressive language (describes reality) from constitutive language (changes institutional reality), and correspondingly distinguishes a descriptive sentence from a constitutive/performative one.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
"I appoint you chairman."
"The meeting is adjourned."
"I declare the parliament in session."
b_rows_sample.statement: Gives performative-utterance examples that create institutional facts under appropriate constitutive rules: 'I appoint you chairman', 'The meeting is adjourned', 'I declare the parliament in session'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: descriptive assertion: 'Alice is President.' / constitutive act: 'Alice is hereby appointed President.'
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes a descriptive assertion ('Alice is President') from a constitutive act ('Alice is hereby appointed President'), arguing the latter is not merely reporting a fact but may, under correct institutional rule and authority, create/change the status -- extending the project's prior generic definition of 'assertion = claim about something'.

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Therefore KnowledgeOS needs:

```text
utterance
+
speaker
+
authority
+
context
+
constitutive rule
+
institutional state
```
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues KnowledgeOS needs to preserve utterance + speaker + authority + context + constitutive rule + institutional state together in order to correctly interpret institutional claims/actions, since a statement like 'Alice is President' being true and 'I declare Alice President' successfully performing an institutional act depend on different conditions (valid appointment vs. speaker authority under constitutive rules).

b_rows_sample.anchor: He distinguishes explicit rules from **background capacities, abilities, dispositions and practices** that agents use to function within institutions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Adopts Searle's 'background' idea (explicit rules vs. background capacities, abilities, dispositions, and practices agents use to function within institutions) as a further reason the Knowledge Space cannot be reduced to explicit documents; e.g. a Constitution does not contain every practical competence required to execute the institution (explicit rules + procedural know-how + social practices + recognized conventions).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 1. A phenomenon/object can receive a status. ... 10. Some utterances are themselves institutional actions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Applies the Zero Lens (removing money, marriage, president, election, government, property, language, constitution) and derives a ten-item residual list of what survives: (1) a phenomenon/object can receive a status; (2) status is assigned relative to a context; (3) collective intentionality can support the assignment; (4) constitutive rules define what counts as what; (5) statuses can create powers, rights and obligations; (6) institutional facts form networks; (7) institutional facts depend on underlying brute facts; (8) some statuses persist through representation and recognition; (9) institutional processes create/change institutional states; (10) some utterances are themselves institutional actions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would add an **Institutional Space**:
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes adding an Institutional Space branch alongside Natural Space and Semantic Space in the Knowledge Space diagram, containing statuses/roles/rights/obligations/powers/institutions, feeding into an epistemic space and agent/group states, which in turn feed Knowledge projections.

b_rows_sample.anchor: StatusFunction(X,Y,C)
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes StatusFunction(X,Y,C) (not 'Institution') as the institutional layer's primitive candidate, associated with collective recognition, rule, authority, power, rights, obligations, context, and time; worked example StatusFunction(X=person, Y=President, C=Republic R) generating rights/obligations/powers/responsibilities, argued to be extremely compatible with the constitutional/governance architecture.

b_notations: X counts as Y in C
